We introduce PerMemBench, the first benchmark that jointly models multi domain interaction histories and cross user heterogeneity in agent use patterns to evaluate personalized memory systems. We further present the first empirical study of memory personalization, proposing session-level storage gating, a lightweight framework that selectively bypasses memory operations for transient sessions. Our study confirms that personalization yields substantial retention gains under perfect gating, yet reveals that accurate gating remains an open and critical challenge. Our benchmark and source code are available at https://github.com/yeonjun-in/PerMemBench.

items.title: Towards Faithful Agentic XAI: A Verification Method and an Open-World Benchmark for Better Model Faithfulness
items.description: arXiv:2605.27879v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) helps users interpret model behavior and identify potential faults. Agentic XAI systems use Large Language Models (LLMs) to make explanations more accessible through natural-language interaction, but they can also produce plausible yet unfaithful explanations. This risk arises because unreliable XAI outputs for complex models can be amplified by LLMs and mislead users. We propose Faithful Agentic XAI (FAX), a verification method that improves the faithfulness of Agentic XAI explanations. FAX decomposes draft explanations into claims and tests them with inherently faithful tools that query the target model directly, filtering unsupported or contradicted claims before final generation. We also introduce CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, an open-world reinforcement learning benchmark with complex policies, diverse goals, and challenging scenarios for assessing model-specific faithfulness. On CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, FAX improves simulation faithfulness from 0.20 for the strongest baseline to 0.46 while maintaining high informativeness, relevance, and fluency. On three tabular benchmarks, FAX performs competitively with prior Agentic XAI baselines, but our analysis shows that these settings can conflate task accuracy with model-specific faithfulness. These findings show that explicit verification is essential for faithful Agentic XAI and that faithfulness benchmarks must be designed to test explanations against the behavior of the target model itself.

items.title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once
items.description: arXiv:2606.06462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmarks provide standardized measures for evaluating and advancing large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). As models improve, existing benchmarks can approach saturation, making it harder to challenge models and distinguish among them. While reusing annotated datasets can reduce data collection and labeling effort, constructing new benchmarks remains labor-intensive, and existing agent-based approaches often target specific tasks or automate only parts of the process. To address these challenges, we introduce BenchHarness, an autonomous harness for end-to-end benchmark customization. It coordinates multiple agents and tools to analyze user requirements, search for suitable datasets, and construct validated benchmarks, with support for refinement based on model performance. To evaluate BenchHarness, we construct 16 benchmarks spanning diverse tasks and modalities. Human review and LLM-as-a-judge assessments indicate high benchmark quality, while evaluations across multiple models reveal challenging tasks and meaningful performance differences. In comparisons with source benchmarks, the generated benchmarks yield lower scores and larger performance gaps, even when the originals approach saturation. BenchHarness thus provides a reusable approach to benchmark construction, supporting informative evaluation as model capabilities and user needs evolve. Our code and benchmarks are publicly available.

items.title: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents
items.description: arXiv:2607.23586v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change. We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

items.title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
items.description: arXiv:2608.07437v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

items.title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
items.description: arXiv:2609.06960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

items.title: SpecRead: A Benchmark for Measuring Whether Language Models Understand Hardware Specifications
items.description: arXiv:2609.33699v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) in hardware design evaluate downstream artifacts such as generated RTL, assertions, or testbenches. When a model fails, it may have misread the specification or understood it and failed to write the code. We present SpecRead, a benchmark that isolates specification comprehension from generation ability. SpecRead v2.2 contains 383 questions over 10 open-source OpenTitan IP blocks in four types: exact retrieval, cross-section reasoning, contradiction detection in mutated specifications, and spec-RTL consistency checking, plus 41 distractor controls and 41 consistent-RTL controls. Type-4 items use real RTL mutations retained only when Icarus Verilog simulation shows a behavioral change. A with-spec vs. without-spec ablation suggests the questions require the excerpt rather than training recall alone, though it does not rule out memorization of the unmutated source text helping a model spot mutations. Ministral-3B scores 33.7% overall (129/383). On t3, verdict-plus-location accuracy is 48.0% with a 51.2% distractor false-positive rate. On t4, the violation-vs.-compliant decision is effectively degenerate (MCC -0.06, balanced accuracy 49.5%), flagging all 41 consistent-RTL controls; location accuracy remains measurable at 79.2%. Layered scoring suggests, as a hypothesis, that the fine-grained violation taxonomy is the hard part, though the category labels are not independently validated. A rule-table prompting intervention on a 60-question sample lowers accuracy on every type except t2 (tied). SpecRead is automatically scorable by deterministic checks, with gray-zone cases counted wrong under the conservative main scoring, regenerable for type-3 items via mutation injection, and built exclusively from public sources.

items.title: Agent Calibration under Deployment Change: Acceptance Contracts, Trajectory Repair, and Adaptation Costs
items.description: arXiv:2609.35149v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An agent can remain operational after a model, tool, or user-context change while losing capabilities required at its destination. We define agent calibration as qualification against a versioned deployment contract. The contract specifies basic capabilities and end-to-end reachability, technical and professional precision, and acceptance by intended users. For each requirement, a source-to-destination map records what must be preserved, transformed, added, or retired. Experts supply benchmarks, positive and negative examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits. These instruments guide changes to prompts and context, tool calls and other harness settings, or an external compact policy while the foundation model remains frozen. Candidate revisions are evaluated against fixed acceptance criteria using independent evidence. We compare the costs of maintaining a harness with and without an external policy, including annotation, training, serving, review, and rework. Three diagnostic audits illustrate the limits of aggregate scores. On a 100-item intent task, each model solved cases the other missed. In a 60-record synthetic financial reporting fixture, five records passed a numeric proxy but failed the reporting contract. In a target-only WebMall snapshot, quota interruptions affected 132 of 171 attempts. These observations motivate paired reruns, checkpoint replay, and separate measurement of repaired and newly failed cases. We specify controlled experiments to test whether calibration increases accepted deliveries at a given cost.

items.title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
items.description: arXiv:2609.35744v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics that reflect expert standards and fix the values correct as of an information cutoff. Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. This expert guidance governs every agent, as prompts and as rules that code enforces, and a Task Bank of reusable criteria carries it across tasks. In long-horizon loops that follow the expert guidance, a writer agent researches every expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, and failures escalate to a human. On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, its rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria, their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark, built from in-house analysts' key questions across 78 tasks and eight asset classes, shows that rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.

items.title: ACTR: Aligning Thoughts and Responses for Multilingual Safety in Reasoning LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2609.37054v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.

items.title: FluidPD: In-Place Elasticity for SLO-Aware Prefill-Decode Disaggregated LLM Serving
items.description: arXiv:2610.06917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prefill-decode (P/D) disaggregation serves the two phases of LLM inference on separate workers, typically with a fixed prefill/decode worker ratio. Real workloads exhibit both short bursts and sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, so a fixed split can violate latency SLOs while capacity sits idle in the other pool. Autoscaling adds capacity, but it reacts slowly, requires spare GPUs, and does not address short-timescale phase imbalance. We present FluidPD, a P/D-disaggregated serving system with SLO-aware in-place elasticity. FluidToken absorbs transient imbalance by offloading a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers that have slack. FluidRole absorbs sustained imbalance by switching running workers between the prefill and decode roles in place, without model reload or engine restart. Both are guided by indices that expose the pressure in each phase before it causes SLO violations. On workloads derived from production Azure traces and ShareGPT conversations with sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment by up to 47.9 percentage points over the best static P/D split for each load, without additional workers.

items.title: Where Can a Decision Model Diagnose HVAC Faults? Reasoning Demand, Physical Representation, and Robustness Under Shift
items.description: arXiv:2610.09937v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

items.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
items.description: arXiv:2610.17584v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

items.title: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
items.description: arXiv:2610.23670v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

items.title: Kairos: Fast and Reliable Symbolic Task Planning for Autonomous Robots
items.description: arXiv:2610.39454v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robots that plan while they act need a task planner that reads the models their designers write, answers within milliseconds, and says what each answer means. Models are written in the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), which has grown from classical planning to durative actions, numeric resources, time windows and continuous change, while planners cover one fragment each and differ in what their failures mean. The contribution in artificial intelligence is Kairos, a single planner, not a portfolio of existing planners, that covers the whole language and derives what each answer guarantees from the search that produced it. We prove when the exhaustion of a search shows that no plan exists, and give a relaxation of temporal tasks that proves unsolvability where temporal search cannot. For the compression of durative actions, we give a criterion on the values that actions read, prove that compression is sound, and show that it is not complete, so its failure is never reported as a proof. An independent validator checks every plan. The engineering application is on-line task planning for robots: Kairos is open source, packaged for the Robot Operating System, and the default planner of a widely used planning framework. On 1,756 public tasks from nine suites, Kairos solves more tasks than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite within 100 milliseconds, 1 second and 30 seconds; it proves ten of eleven unsolvable tasks, and handles each of the seventeen language features probed, where no other planner handles more than eight.

items.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
items.description: arXiv:2610.41183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. In this paper, we develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline combining program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, and independent verification. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions from specifications that supplied no family formula. Researcher-directed analysis with a language model led to a general construction and proof drafts, which the researchers revised and checked. The resulting family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ exists for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$; Lean checks its formalized algebraic core. With entanglement lifting, it closes 54 listed table gaps. The evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten DRAT-checked nonexistence results, family implementations and preserved search programs. Controlled studies test how research proposals interact with program generation. Under a mutation-and-restart proposal, iterative evolution improves normalized success-curve area in all ten paired runs and raises success at excluded lengths $n=13,15$ from 13.4% to 62.5% and from 0.9% to 33.4%, respectively. The benefit depends on the proposal. Selected programs combine the proposed moves with objective and restart-counter changes. The pipeline connects finite computational discoveries to a proved family and independently checkable constructions.

items.title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
items.description: arXiv:2611.04241v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

items.title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
items.description: arXiv:2611.11658v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

items.title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
items.description: arXiv:2611.13487v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

items.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
items.description: arXiv:2611.14949v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce RSI-PDEbench, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

items.title: $\varepsilon$-WM: Error-Driven Dynamics Adaptation across Fast--Slow Timescales for World Modeling
items.description: arXiv:2611.15215v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to balance three key requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, rapidly correcting sudden changes; stability, avoiding lasting model updates from transient disturbances; and persistence, retaining adapted dynamics during the observation-free open-loop rollout. Inspired by multi-timescale predictive coding in the human brain, we propose $\varepsilon$-WM, a world model that adapts to unknown dynamics through error-driven corrections across fast and slow timescales. $\varepsilon$-WM incorporates three novel features: 1) Multiple internal experts (MiE) emulate neural pathway reweighting, each combining a fixed base expert with fast--slow adaptation networks. 2) Fast--slow timescale adaptation captures distinct adaptation dynamics: fast states respond rapidly and decay, whereas slow states accumulate corrections and persist. 3) Predictive correction uses prediction errors to update fast and slow states and reweight experts without gradients. During open-loop rollout, each expert feeds back its own predictions, and $\varepsilon$-WM aggregates their outputs through adaptive weighting. Extensive experiments show $\varepsilon$-WM has a consistently lower multi-step mean error than all ten baselines on six datasets, verifying the effectiveness of each feature.

items.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
items.description: arXiv:2611.22374v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

items.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
items.description: arXiv:2611.28202v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across closed and open-source models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

items.title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.28356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

items.title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks
items.description: arXiv:2611.30281v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B-14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs), and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.

items.title: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.30545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In text to image AI models, fixing the prompt and the random seed is widely assumed to fix the image. We show that it does not on GPUs. We evaluate six text-to-image models (diffusion and autoregressive) under four numerical precisions and quantizations on three GPU types (RTX A6000, RTX 6000 Ada, and H100 NVL), across up to 100 prompts per set for all six models. For each configuration we compare, with the prompt and seed fixed, the image generated alone with the image generated inside a batch, and we also compare across GPUs. Every replay control reported here is bit-exact, so the variation is not random noise: the execution setting, mainly the batch composition and the GPU, decides the output. The effect is large and model dependent. Structural similarity between the single-image and the batched output falls to 0.580 for an autoregressive model in bf16 and to 0.551 with int8. For a second autoregressive model in bf16 it falls to 0.261 with sampled decoding and to 0.229 with greedy decoding, and for an fp8 diffusion model to 0.68. A diffusion model in bf16 stays close to the batch-1 output (0.96-0.98) but changes every image. In most cases the batched image is a different but equally valid image; in some, such as prompts with digits and counters, it is visibly worse. Cross-GPU differences are of the same order as the batch effect: for one autoregressive model in bf16 compared across two GPU architectures (RTX 6000 Ada versus RTX A6000), no image is bit-identical and the cross-GPU LPIPS (0.355 to 0.383) matches the batch effect within one GPU (0.347 to 0.381). The consequences are direct: seeds do not make results reproducible, benchmarks and image-quality comparisons that mix batch sizes or hardware can be biased, and safety audits and A/B tests on generated images need the serving setup reported.

items.title: Fine-Grained Instruction-Guided Graph Reasoning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
items.description: arXiv:2503.11006v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision and Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to traverse complex environments by following natural language instructions, demanding accurate alignment between visual observations and linguistic guidance. To address these challenges, we propose a fine grained instruction guided graph reasoning framework (FIGR) that enhances both spatial representation and instruction understanding during navigation. Specifically, an observation graph interaction mechanism is introduced to disentangle angular and visual cues while strengthening directed edge representations through geometric embedding, enabling more reliable spatial reasoning within the navigation graph. The key detail guidance module is implemented as Adaptive Open Vocabulary Guidance (AOVG), where a contextual role parser dynamically identifies location, object, spatial relation, and other contextual cues. This design avoids exact string matching and supports previously unseen entities and compositional expressions. For multilingual instructions, a Multilingual Semantic Adapter (MSA) maps language-specific representations into a shared navigation-semantic space. By jointly integrating structured graph reasoning with instruction critical semantic cues, the proposed approach significantly improves the agent ability to follow complex navigation instructions. On the validation-unseen splits, FIGR achieves 67 SPL on R2R and 64.8 sDTW on RxR, exceeding SPENav by 1 percentage point in SPL and PRET by 2.4 points in sDTW, respectively.

items.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
items.description: arXiv:2506.00058v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.

items.title: VITA: Vision-to-Action Flow Matching Policy
items.description: arXiv:2507.13231v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conventional flow matching and diffusion-based policies sample via iterative denoising from standard noise distributions (e.g., Gaussian), and require conditioning modules to repeatedly incorporate visual information during the generative process, incurring substantial time and memory overhead. To reduce the complexity, we develop VITA (Vision-To-Action flow matching policy), a noise-free and conditioning-free flow matching policy learning framework that directly flows from visual representations to latent actions. Since the source of the flow is visually grounded, VITA eliminates the need for visual conditioning during generation. As expected, bridging vision and action is challenging, because actions are lower-dimensional, less structured, and sparser than visual representations; moreover, flow matching requires the source and target to have the same dimensionality. To overcome this, we introduce an action autoencoder that maps raw actions into a structured latent space aligned with visual latents, trained jointly with flow matching. To further prevent latent action space collapse during end-to-end training, we propose flow latent decoding, which anchors the latent generation process by backpropagating the action reconstruction loss through the flow matching ODE (ordinary differential equation) solving steps. We evaluate VITA on 9 simulation and 5 real-world tasks from ALOHA and Robomimic. VITA achieves 1.9x faster inference compared to conventional flow matching with conditioning modules, while outperforming or matching state-of-the-art policies. Project page: https://ucd-dare.github.io/VITA/.

items.title: Rational Adversaries and the Maintenance of Fragility: A Game-Theoretic Theory of Rational Stagnation
items.description: arXiv:2510.22232v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cooperative systems often remain in persistently suboptimal yet stable states. This paper explains such "rational stagnation" as an equilibrium sustained by a rational adversary whose utility follows the principle of potential loss, $u_{D} = U_{ideal} - U_{actual}$. Starting from the Prisoner's Dilemma, we show that the transformation $u_{i}' = a\,u_{i} + b\,u_{j}$ and the ratio of mutual recognition $w = b/a$ generate a fragile cooperation band $[w_{\min},\,w_{\max}]$ where both (C,C) and (D,D) are equilibria. Extending to a dynamic model with stochastic cooperative payoffs $R_{t}$ and intervention costs $(C_{c},\,C_{m})$, a Bellman-style analysis yields three strategic regimes: immediate destruction, rational stagnation, and intervention abandonment. The appendix further generalizes the utility to a reference-dependent nonlinear form and proves its stability under reference shifts, ensuring robustness of the framework. Applications to social-media algorithms and political trust illustrate how adversarial rationality can deliberately preserve fragility.

items.title: IntentMiner: Intent Inversion Attack via Tool Call Analysis in the Model Context Protocol
items.description: arXiv:2512.14166v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) into Agentic AI has established the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the standard for connecting reasoning engines with external tools. Although this decoupled architecture fosters modularity, it simultaneously shatters the traditional trust boundary. We uncover a novel privacy vector inherent to this paradigm: the Intent Inversion Attack. We show that semi-honest third-party MCP servers can accurately reconstruct users' underlying intents by leveraging only authorized metadata (e.g., function signatures, arguments, and receipts), effectively bypassing the need for raw query access. To quantify this threat, we introduce IntentMiner. Unlike statistical approaches, IntentMiner employs a hierarchical semantic parsing strategy that performs step-level intent reconstruction by analyzing tool functions, parameter entities, and result feedback in an orthogonal manner. Experiments on the ToolACE benchmark reveal that IntentMiner achieves a semantic alignment of over 85% with original queries, substantially surpassing LLM baselines. This work exposes a critical endogenous vulnerability: without semantic obfuscation, executing functions requires the transparency of intent, thereby challenging the privacy foundations of next-generation AI agents.

items.title: interwhen: A Generalizable Framework for Steering Reasoning Models with Test-time Verification
items.description: arXiv:2602.11202v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reasoning models produce long traces of intermediate decisions and tool calls, making test-time verification important for ensuring correctness. Existing approaches either verify only the final answer, which misses early errors, or rely on branch-and-verify strategies that explore multiple trajectories. We introduce interwhen, a single-trajectory verification framework that steers model behavior by providing feedback on intermediate reasoning traces. It addresses two key challenges. First, given a set of verifiers, obtaining verifiable states from the reasoning trace typically requires prompt engineering or external task decomposition into fixed steps. Instead, we propose a monitoring system that periodically polls the reasoning trace and forks inference of the reasoning model to recover intermediate states. Verifiers are run asynchronously alongside generation, adding negligible overhead on correct executions and intervening only when violations occur. Second, beyond math and code, a central challenge for process verification is the scarcity of verifiers. interwhen addresses this through automatic verifier synthesis from natural-language policy documents. Given a policy, it can generate code-based verifiers, including provably correct verifiers in Lean and z3. Together, these contributions yield a plug-and-play test-time verification system that can improve task completion and policy compliance of any reasoning agent. On reasoning benchmarks where policies encode mathematical or logical constraints, interwhen achieves near-perfect accuracy for reasoning models using a fraction of the tokens of baselines. On agentic benchmarks with policy-based verifier generation, it enables improvements in task quality for SLMs without any finetuning, e.g., task completion rate of Qwen3-30B jumps from 32% to 87% on the telecom domain in tau2-bench. Code at https://github.com/microsoft/interwhen.

items.title: AESP: A Human-Sovereign Economic Protocol for AI Agents with Privacy-Preserving Settlement
items.description: arXiv:2603.00318v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As AI agents increasingly perform economic tasks on behalf of humans, a fundamental tension arises between agent autonomy and human control over financial assets. We present the Agent Economic Sovereignty Protocol (AESP), a layered protocol in which agents transact autonomously at machine speed on crypto-native infrastructure while remaining cryptographically bound to human-defined governance boundaries. AESP enforces the invariant that agents are economically capable but never economically sovereign through five mechanisms: (1) a deterministic eight-check policy engine with tiered escalation; (2) human-in-the-loop review with automatic, explicit, and biometric tiers; (3) EIP-712 dual-signed commitments with escrow; (4) HKDF-based context-isolated privacy with batched consolidation; and (5) an ACE-GF-based cryptographic substrate. We formalize two testable hypotheses on security coverage and latency overhead, and specify a complete evaluation methodology with baselines and ablation design. The protocol is implemented as an open-source TypeScript SDK (208 tests, ten modules) with interoperability via MCP and A2A.

items.title: First-Class Relationships as a Representation Threshold: Identity, Time, Confidence, and Causation
items.description: arXiv:2603.13603v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Operational records -- who may access what, what changed, what caused an incident -- consist of relationships that involve several parties, hold for a period, are believed with some confidence, and cause one another. We ask what a representation must provide to store such records directly. We state four storage requirements: n-ary relationships with attributes, temporal validity, confidence with an evidential basis, and causal links between relationships. Under our definitions, each requires relationships to have identity: every relationship is stored, fetched and queried as an object with its own key. Confidence with an evidential basis and causal links also require composition: any relationship can take part in another. With n-ary relationships, either one therefore requires first-class relationships, which are identified, carry attributes, and compose at every arity. Conversely, first-class relationships suffice for all four. They are thus a threshold, and it belongs to the relationship construct, not to the data model around it: where a model's own construct falls short, every representation meeting n-ary relationships together with evidence-backed confidence or causal links builds a first-class construct from other parts, as our SQL implementation does. We place SQL, property graphs, RDF 1.2 and TypeDB relative to the threshold, and present the Attributed Temporal Causal Hypergraph (ATCH), which meets all four requirements with query operators for each.

items.title: Architecture-Agnostic Feature Synergy for Universal Defense Against Heterogeneous Generative Threats
items.description: arXiv:2603.14860v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI deployment poses unprecedented challenges to content safety and privacy. However, existing defense mechanisms are often tailored to specific architectures (e.g., Diffusion Models or GANs), creating fragile "defense silos" that fail against heterogeneous generative threats. This paper identifies a fundamental optimization barrier in naive pixel-space ensemble strategies: due to divergent objective functions, pixel-level gradients from heterogeneous generators become statistically orthogonal, causing destructive interference. To overcome this, we observe that despite disparate low-level mechanisms, high-level feature representations of generated content exhibit alignment across architectures. Based on this, we propose the Architecture-Agnostic Targeted Feature Synergy (ATFS) framework. By introducing a target guidance image, ATFS reformulates multi-model defense as a unified feature space alignment task, enabling intrinsic gradient alignment without complex rectification. Extensive experiments show ATFS achieves SOTA protection in heterogeneous scenarios (e.g., Diffusion+GAN). It converges rapidly, reaching over 90% performance within 40 iterations, and maintains strong attack potency even under tight perturbation budgets. The framework seamlessly extends to unseen architectures (e.g., VQ-VAE) by switching the feature extractor, and demonstrates robust resistance to JPEG compression and scaling. Being computationally efficient and lightweight, ATFS offers a viable pathway to dismantle defense silos and enable universal generative security. Code and models are open-sourced for reproducibility.

items.title: A Framework for Closed-Loop Robotic Assembly, Alignment and Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems
items.description: arXiv:2603.21496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robotic automation has transformed scientific workflows in domains such as chemistry and materials science, yet free-space optics, which is a high-precision domain, remains largely manual. Optical systems impose strict spatial and angular tolerances, and their performance is governed by tightly coupled physical parameters, making generalizable automation particularly challenging. In this work, we present a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems. Our approach integrates a hierarchical computer vision system, optimization routines, and custom-built tools to achieve this functionality. As a representative demonstration, we perform the fully autonomous construction of a tabletop laser cavity from randomly distributed components. The system performs several tasks such as laser beam centering, spatial alignment of multiple beams, resonator alignment, laser mode selection, and self-recovery from induced misalignment and disturbances. By achieving closed-loop autonomy for highly sensitive optical systems, this work establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.

items.title: AI Lifecycle-Aware Feasibility Framework for Split-RIC Orchestration in NTN O-RAN
items.description: arXiv:2603.23252v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) is constrained by the joint limits of satellite Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP), feeder-link capacity, and orbital connectivity, which directly affect O-RAN closed-loop control and AI lifecycle management. This paper studies the feasibility of distributing the O-RAN intelligence across Ground, LEO, and GEO segments through three representative deployments: (i) Ground-Centric control with telemetry streaming, (ii) a ground-LEO Split-RIC with on-board inference and store-and-forward model refresh, and (iii) GEO-LEO multi-layer control enabled by inter-satellite links. For each deployment, we derive closed-form expressions for lifecycle energy, near-real-time control latency, and model-refresh latency, while explicitly enforcing power-feasible spaceborne computational throughput. Pairwise analytical boundaries and numerical sensitivity analysis over telemetry volume, feeder-link conditions, inference workload, model longevity, and orbital waiting time identify the operating regions in which different placements are energetically preferable or satisfy model-refresh requirements. The results show that the architecture choice is inherently lifecycle- and constraint-dependent, providing decision-enabling primitives for Service Management and Orchestration (SMO) level AI placement and lifecycle orchestration in NTN O-RAN.

items.title: On Semiotic-Grounded Interpretive Evaluation of Generative Art
items.description: arXiv:2604.08641v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpretation is essential to deciphering the language of art: audiences communicate with artists by recovering meaning from visual artifacts. However, current Generative Art (GenArt) evaluators primarily emphasize surface-level image quality or literal prompt adherence, failing to assess the deeper symbolic or contextual meaning intended by the creator. We formalize this observation using Peircean computational semiotic theory that models Human-GenArt Interaction (HGI) as cascaded semiosis. This framework reveals that artistic meaning is conveyed through iconic, symbolic, and indexical modes, whereas appearance-centered evaluators tend to emphasize the iconic mode. Building on this account, we propose SemJudge, an interpretation-centric evaluation framework that uses a Hierarchical Semiosis Graph (HSG) to reconstruct meaning conveyance from prompt to generated artifact. Experiments on an interpretation-intensive benchmark, SemiosisArt, show that SemJudge aligns more closely with human judgments than existing baselines. User studies further demonstrate that SemJudge produces deeper, more insightful artistic interpretations. We hope these findings pave the way for GenArt to move beyond the generation of "pretty" images toward a medium capable of understanding and expressing complex human experience. Project page: https://github.com/songrise/SemJudge

items.title: Exascale Multi-Task Graph Foundation Models for Imbalanced, Multi-Fidelity Atomistic Data
items.description: arXiv:2604.15380v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present an exascale workflow for atomistic graph foundation models using HydraGNN. Multi-task learning enables joint training across 16 heterogeneous first-principles datasets representing over 467 million unique structures (over 544 million cumulative branch records) and covering 85+ elements. A shared graph neural network backbone with dataset-specific prediction heads accommodates the strongly imbalanced, multi-source, multi-fidelity corpus, supported by scalable ADIOS2/DDStore data management. Composition-conditioned weighting combines source-specific predictions into a single deployable model. Six large-scale hyperparameter optimization campaigns, followed by resource-aware continual training on 2,048 Frontier nodes, identify PaiNN as the lead architecture under a fixed computational budget. We evaluate scalability across Frontier, Aurora, and Perlmutter and characterize transfer across twelve down-stream tasks, including comparisons with pretrained UMA and MACE models under different adaptation strategies. These results reveal task-dependent transfer benefits and highlight the importance of matching adaptation strategies to downstream applications. Finally, we assess inference optimizations and BF16/FP32/FP64 precision tradeoffs, achieving the screening of 1.1 billion atomistic structures in approximately 50 seconds on Frontier. Together, these results establish a scalable framework for multi-source atomistic foundation model training, evaluation, and high-throughput deployment, thereby allowing for a fast and reliable exploration of vast chemical design spaces that are otherwise inaccessible to first-principles methods

items.title: A Threshold Model of Fault Propagation in AI-Native Software Ecosystems
items.description: arXiv:2604.19827v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When many coding agents work in one repository at once, software engineers are left to judge a collective through its parts. Review examines one change at a time, yet a change can incorporate a fault introduced by another, and repairing the originating change then no longer repairs the repository. To keep human judgment at the centre of agentic software development, we need models of what agents do together. This paper joins complexity theory with software evolution to build one. We model how a fault spreads among open changes as a branching process over contention, the relation between two changes that are open at the same time and modify a common file. As with the reproduction number of an epidemic, spread sustains itself once each faulty change passes the fault, on average, to more than one other. Each repository has a reference threshold, the crossing probability per contention link above which spread would sustain itself in a random graph with the repository's contention degrees. We reconstructed contention among 33,105 agent-authored pull requests in 2,731 repositories. Thirteen repositories with reference thresholds below 5% contained 42.5% of the changes. There, a fault that crossed one contention link in twenty would sustain spread under the model. The structural conditions for propagation are in place where much agent-authored work happens. Reviewing each change separately cannot reveal these conditions. Engineers also need to know where concurrent work exposes a repository to spreading faults, which they can compute from records they already keep.

items.title: GRASP: Graph Agentic Search over Propositions for Multi-hop Question Answering
items.description: arXiv:2605.16598v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agentic retrieval improves multi-hop question answering by giving language models autonomy to iteratively gather evidence. Recent work augments these systems with knowledge graphs for structured traversal, but this combination introduces significant cost: expensive graph construction at index time and compounding token usage at inference time. We introduce Graph Agentic Search over Propositions (GRASP), an agentic system that simultaneously optimizes for high accuracy and minimal token usage in multi-hop question answering. Rather than executing a rigid, singular query, GRASP actively coordinates its retrieval strategy by decomposing multi-hop queries into dependency-aware plans. This enables GRASP to dynamically scale the number of sub-agents according to the complexity of the problem. Each sub-agent resolves its single-hop query by exploring a novel three-layer hierarchical graph of entities, propositions, and passages, using the entity layer for targeted traversal and the proposition layer for high-recall passage retrieval via reciprocal-rank voting. We evaluate GRASP on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA, and HotpotQA under two settings: open-corpus retrieval and extended context reasoning (LongBench). GRASP achieves the highest QA accuracy in the open retrieval setting on MuSiQue and 2Wiki while using 40-50 percent fewer tokens than IRCoT+HippoRAG2. Furthermore, GRASP leads on EM and F1 across all three datasets in the LongBench setting while using 30 percent fewer tokens than the next most accurate method. Finally, we introduce success economy - the amortized token cost per correct answer, weighted by difficulty - and advocate for efficiency-aware evaluation as a standard practice for agentic QA.

items.title: A Tool to Map AI Programs in the U.S.: A Snapshot from April 2026 and an Analysis of Requirements for AI Majors and Minors
items.description: arXiv:2606.12428v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we locate and analyze existing undergraduate Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs in the United States in Spring 2026, creating a historic record at a time of great change in this area. To create this record, we developed a tool to detect, scrape, and display data from 361 undergraduate AI programs--majors, minors, concentrations, and certificates--at 4-year universities. Our tool, available at https://cicmap.ai, searched 563 institutions to locate these programs, a sample that represents 87% of all undergraduate Computer Science (CS) graduates in the U.S in 2025. This tool allows prospective students, guidance counselors, administrators, and faculty to easily access AI program requirements and is designed to continually update as new programs emerge. To the best of our knowledge, this survey represents the most comprehensive snapshot of the state of AI programs in the U.S. to date. With this work we offer three important contributions: 1) a record of AI programs in the U.S. at a time of great upheaval; 2) a tool to explore AI programs and their requirements; and 3) an analysis of the courses required for 66 AI majors and 87 AI minors. Our analysis of majors and minors shows great variability in the size and the requirements of these degrees, but we note two takeaways. First, not all majors require a general AI course, but if they don't, they do require a Machine Learning (ML) course. Second, more than a third of majors require an Ethics in AI course but only 24% of minors do.

items.title: Instant NuRec: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstruction for Driving Scene Simulation
items.description: arXiv:2607.14203v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D simulation platforms are critical for autonomous driving because they enable end-to-end policy evaluation, thereby reducing development costs and improving safety. In recent years, neural simulation has become predominant, with methods such as NuRec playing a central role; however, these methods remain relatively slow and typically require per-scene tuning. In this work, we present Instant NuRec, a feed-forward neural reconstruction model that turns a short multi-view driving log into a fully simulatable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) world in a single forward pass. The model accepts multi-view input from a calibrated camera rig and emits a layered output consisting of static and dynamic 3DGS layers, a sky cubemap, and per-camera ISP corrections, while providing native support for non-pinhole camera models via 3DGUT. It reconstructs a 10-20-second multi-camera scene in roughly 1.5 seconds and achieves a PSNR on the Waymo Open Dataset that is 2.01 dB above the strongest evaluated baseline. Instant NuRec is deeply integrated into NuRec and is compatible with AlpaSim for closed-loop simulation.

items.title: AiFlow: Construction-to-Retirement Conformance for Versioned LLM Services
items.description: arXiv:2608.00558v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A live update can preserve the topology and output of a large language model (LLM) workflow while bypassing a filter's queue and concurrency limits. A background task can use the old version after its caller returns. AiFlow links construction, invocation and retirement through an executable contract. Each admitted request captures an action bound to the checked operators. The service certifies the call's terminal outcome and the release of its registered work. Once new calls can no longer capture the version, the owner checks these certificates and remaining local resources before retirement. Strict publication pauses admission while old calls drain. Deferred publication can admit calls to the successor before its predecessor retires. We evaluated two stateless linear workflows in one Java virtual machine. Under strict publication, we repeated three injected fault scenarios three times per check configuration. An observation counted as contained if neither unguarded execution nor premature replacement occurred. With construction or completion checking alone, six of nine fault observations met this criterion. With both checks, all nine did. A separately implemented coordinator matched AiFlow on the lifecycle outcome, service call count and reclamation decision in all 24 tested pairs. With updates every 400 ms, deferred publication met the 500 ms deadline more often at both loads. We measured the share of all offered requests that met the deadline on the latest scheduled version due at return. Strict publication led at 80 requests/s and deferred publication at 20 requests/s. Both policies use the same local evidence for retirement.

items.title: Unified CT and MRI Pancreas Segmentation for Label-Efficient Cross-Modality Subregion Transfer
items.description: arXiv:2609.13043v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robust medical image segmentation across imaging modalities is challenging because of large differences in appearance and intensity distributions. Models trained on a single modality often show substantial performance drops when applied to unseen domains. In this work, we develop a unified 3D pancreas segmentation framework that applies domain-adversarial learning to 4,604 heterogeneous CT and MRI scans to learn anatomical representations. A shared nnU-Net encoder-decoder is trained for whole-pancreas segmentation, with a latent domain discriminator encouraging CT-MRI feature alignment. The learned encoder is subsequently transferred to pancreatic head-body-tail segmentation using limited MRI-only subregion annotations. An average Dice score of 87.31% on the in-distribution test set and Dice scores ranging from 84.20% to 88.09% across external OOD datasets were achieved in whole pancreas segmentation. Dice scores of 80.53% on MRI and 83.05% on CT were achieved for downstream subregion segmentation, without using CT subregion annotations. These results demonstrate that a unified anatomical representation can support both cross-modality pancreas segmentation and label-efficient downstream transfer.

items.title: TryOnReward: Learning Foveated Consistency for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Virtual Try-On
items.description: arXiv:2609.13259v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to dress a person with the reference garment, producing visually reasonable results aligned with human preferences. Turning this preference-oriented goal into an actionable objective relies on a scoring function aligned with human taste. However, classic fidelity metrics exhibit weak correlation with human judgments, and generic VLMs fail to provide the discriminative granularity demanded by try-on quality evaluation, which hinges on faithfully preserving garment and person details. This shortcoming is further exacerbated in the reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) optimization and leads to severe reward hacking. To this end, we present TryOnReward, a fine-grained reward model tailored for VTON. Built on a vision-language backbone, it adopts a foveation calibration objective that grounds each quality dimension in the relevant region to avoid global shortcut learning. Meanwhile, TryOnReward jointly optimizes pairwise preferences and per-dimension quality scores via margin-aware supervision, leveraging both relative and absolute quality signals. For model training and evaluation, we build TryOnRank-100K, a human-annotated per-dimension rating dataset, alongside TryOn-Bench and TryOnRewardBench, two benchmarks covering diverse real scenarios. Extensive experiments confirm that our proposed TryOnReward significantly outperforms generic judges in human preference alignment, and when serving as the RFT reward function, it consistently yields human-preferred try-on results across multiple baselines.

items.title: Sparse-WAM: Accelerating World Action Models via Action-Guided Sparse Imagination
items.description: arXiv:2609.38984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video models to improve generalization in robot control by jointly predicting future visual states and actions. This capability comes at a substantial inference cost, as dense future-frame tokens are repeatedly processed during denoising. Prior methods address this by token pruning that prioritizes visual fidelity to reduce denoising costs in video diffusion models. However, these methods do not use action relevance to determine which future-frame tokens to retain during joint denoising in WAMs. In this paper, we propose Sparse-WAM, a training-free framework for action-guided sparse imagination that selectively processes future-frame tokens to accelerate WAM inference. We observe substantial overlap in the spatial distribution of attention from action tokens to future-frame tokens (action-to-future attention) between consecutive denoising steps, despite continued updates to the future representations. Motivated by this, we develop Action-Guided Token Selection to retain frame-specific action-relevant regions together with cross-frame context. However, a naive implementation can incur attention-scoring and token-packing overhead that offsets the computational savings from pruning. We therefore introduce Pilot, an efficient engine that reduces sparse inference overhead through lightweight scoring and cross-step reuse of token selections. On LIBERO with FastWAM-Joint and RoboLab-120 with Cosmos 3 Edge, Sparse-WAM achieves inference speedups of approximately $2.0\times$ and $1.8\times$, respectively, over dense eager inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, while largely preserving task performance.

items.title: VisionQ: Benchmarking VLM Judges on Criterion-Specific Comparisons of Computer Vision Method Outputs
items.description: arXiv:2610.00666v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Qualitative comparison figures in computer vision papers are commonly established to illustrate which method's output is best on a named criterion, such as visual sharpness or surface complexity. VisionQ investigates this important part of computer vision work beyond human judgment towards objective vision-language models (VLMs) as judges. From 1,409 CVPR and ICCV papers, it creates blind multiple-choice questions, each testing one criterion, with the correct answer based on the authors' claimed best result. The best of 21 judges aligns with the authors' claims on 69% of questions, against 32% by chance. Yet it keeps most of its accuracy without the criterion and changes its answers when the options are reordered. Trained on every option order of a larger question set, our VisionQ-Judge raises accuracy on unseen papers from 50% to 61%. The paper highlights the potential of VLM judges to provide objective, criterion-specific comparisons across a broad range of computer vision methods in the past, present, and future. Data, weights and code are available at https://huggingface.co/visionq-review and https://github.com/ReML-AI/visionq.

items.title: AffectWorld: Benchmarking Emotion-Driven Future World Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2610.18305v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely untested. We introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion - Action - World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 223 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define seven metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of eight SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos 3) required world-state change scores of 0.064-0.240 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions.
