AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states\footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AffectWorld-Benchmark-370C/}.

items.title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
items.description: arXiv:2611.08657v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

items.title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
items.description: arXiv:2611.12603v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

items.title: DuoJEPA: Cross-Modal Translation Between Unaligned Self-Supervised Embedding Spaces
items.description: arXiv:2611.15968v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. DuoJEPA trains one encoder per modality with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective and appends to each encoder a single transformer layer that translates its embedding into the other encoder's space, supervised by a contrastive objective computed entirely within that target space. No loss term compares the two own spaces directly, although the encoders are optimised jointly through the translation objective. In our experiments, the translator's residual connections determine where the cross-modal pressure is absorbed: with a residual translator the two encoders become directly aligned, whereas with a skipless (residual-free) translator a paired-cosine test detects no alignment in the final models, and at most a weak one in the ablations, at comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space. We evaluate DuoJEPA on two modality pairs that differ in nearly every respect. On chest radiographs and reports from CheXpert Plus, it attains a zero-shot AUC of 86.6 and a cross-modal retrieval score of 78.5, compared with 60.0 and 64.2 for our reimplementation of LeVLJEPA with the same encoders and data. On Sentinel-2 optical and Sentinel-1 radar imagery, the frozen encoders fall within the range of published Sentinel foundation models under our reproduction of the Copernicus-Bench linear-probe protocol, the translator retrieves the paired image of the other sensor among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases, and a patch-level extension transfers the within-image similarity structure of the scene.

items.title: ReliaGuard: Reconstruction-Aware Watermarking for Source Attribution and Blind Edit Localization
items.description: arXiv:2611.16368v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative image editing can reconstruct the background outside the requested edit, weakening spatial watermark evidence even when the source identifier remains recoverable. This creates an ambiguity for blind localization: a weak watermark response may indicate either an intended edit or background reconstruction. We propose ReliaGuard, a reconstruction-aware watermarking framework that addresses this ambiguity through reconstruction-stable evidence writing and coarse-to-fine blind reading. The writer aligns keyed feature responses in the protected image and its variational autoencoder reconstruction while preserving a frozen source-attribution channel. A quantization-aware projection bounds the distortion of the released eight-bit image. The reader combines keyed responses with image context to refine a base localization map, then integrates native-resolution detail with multiscale features to estimate the edit region. It is trained on paired observations before and after image processing and requires only the received image and key at inference. On 300 source images and 900 editing cases from three domains, ReliaGuard achieves intersection-over-union scores of 85.61% for complete editing outputs and 94.90% for locally spliced outputs at thresholds calibrated to a nominal 1% background false-positive rate on complete outputs. The former exceeds the strongest baseline by 45.02 percentage points, while decoded identifier-bit accuracy reaches 100% in both conditions. Across seven image-processing families, the corresponding localization scores remain 81.01% and 86.49%, with identifier-bit accuracies of 92.76% and 92.79%. These results show that reconstruction-aware writing and contextual reading can jointly support source attribution and edit localization under generative editing and subsequent image processing.

items.title: AI for Parameter Selection in Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization
items.description: arXiv:2611.18307v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) methods provide a way to compute molecular ground-state energies, but their accuracy and runtime depend sensitively on configuration choices such as the subspace dimension, propagation timestep, and the allocation of a fixed sampling budget across circuits, for which no formal selection method exists. In this work, we explore whether oracle models can predict the quantum runtime and approximation error from the Hamiltonian and the candidate configuration. Using synthetic Hamiltonians with controllable spectral properties, we show that machine-learned models can map a Hamiltonian directly to the best-ranked configuration within a predefined grid for the SKQD algorithm, validated against classical Krylov propagation, achieving strong rank correlations between true and predicted error and runtime, Spearman $\rho = 0.969$ and $\rho = 0.905$, respectively. Extending the approach to 50 molecular Hamiltonians (20-50 qubits), with reference ground-state energies from classical calculations, we train regressors that predict the simulation error and runtime for a given molecule--configuration pair ahead of execution, and classifiers to distinguish, from 600 SqDRIFT quantum-hardware runs, whether a configuration achieves a ground-state energy within chemical accuracy ($1.6\times10^{-3}$ Ha $\approx 1$ kcal/mol). For the molecular Hamiltonians, the models additionally provide an a priori feasibility and resource estimate, predicting whether a molecule can reach chemical accuracy on current hardware and at what runtime, thus correctly classifying held-out molecules at the molecule level, achieving balanced accuracy 61.8% in-distribution and 100% for five larger held-out molecules.

items.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
items.description: arXiv:2611.22138v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

items.title: Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework
items.description: arXiv:2611.28082v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Open-weight models advance transparency, research, and innovation, and spread the benefits of AI more widely. They also carry distinct risks. A release cannot be undone, safeguards can be removed through fine-tuning, and no single party can monitor use or withdraw the model. Managing these risks therefore requires an approach tailored to open release. This framework addresses the governance challenge at the heart of that choice. Co-developed by Concordia AI and Z AI, it adapts the full risk management lifecycle, from risk assessment to mitigation and governance, to the unique properties of open-weight models. This document does not resolve every tension between openness and safety. Rather, it provides the first comprehensive, evidence-based foundation for navigating these tensions. As frontier open-weight releases accelerate, risk management best practice and standards are urgently needed. We invite researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society to build on this framework and advance the science and practice of open-weight AI governance.

items.title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts
items.description: arXiv:2611.28732v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools. Project page at https://entangle-robotics.github.io/

items.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
items.description: arXiv:2611.29162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

items.title: RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act
items.description: arXiv:2611.30111v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user says "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.

items.title: RoboAda: Adapting Frozen Robot Policies at Test Time to Physics They Cannot See
items.description: arXiv:2611.30209v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.

items.title: Too Smart for Its Own Good? Cognitive Fidelity and Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners
items.description: arXiv:2611.34042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based interactive learner simulators are increasingly used in educational applications, including teacher training and tutoring system development. A critical requirement for those simulations is cognitive fidelity: the simulated learner should maintain the assigned knowledge, misconceptions, and reasoning procedures throughout interaction. However, LLMs may express knowledge or problem-solving skills beyond the assigned learner's cognitive status, a phenomenon we refer to as competence leakage. In this exploratory study, we examine 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner simulator transcripts across three learning scenarios and identify over-competence as a prominent direction of cognitive-profile misalignment during interaction. We then investigate the recurrence of previously observed competence leakage cases under four matched-trigger evaluation protocols, ranging from isolated questioning to multi-turn interactions, across five model configurations. Overall, we observe higher violation recurrence under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering. More capable models generally show lower recurrence, whereas increased reasoning effort does not consistently improve cognitive fidelity and is even associated with slightly higher recurrence under multi-turn protocols in our matched-model comparison. These findings provide exploratory evidence of competence leakage phenomena in interactive learner simulation and suggest that single-turn question-answering type of evaluations alone may be insufficient, motivating the development of more systematic and reliable multi-turn protocols for evaluating cognitive fidelity in learner simulation.

items.title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
items.description: arXiv:2611.34044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.

items.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
items.description: arXiv:2611.34090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.

items.title: From Data Room to Report: End-to-End AI Support for M&A Legal Due Diligence
items.description: arXiv:2611.34120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.

items.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
items.description: arXiv:2611.34131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The bestseller D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and na\"ive Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.

items.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
items.description: arXiv:2611.34137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.

items.title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
items.description: arXiv:2611.34179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.

items.title: Lightweight Reasoning Transfer via Chain-of-Thought Vector Projection
items.description: arXiv:2611.34183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from large language models to smaller ones often requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. We study projected cross-model Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Vector transfer, a two-stage approach that keeps both models frozen. First, we learn a task-level CoT Vector in the teacher using dataset-provided solution traces and final-answer supervision. We then train a lightweight linear projector to map the fixed vector into a smaller student's residual space. Student-side training uses only final-answer cross-entropy on a small subset of task training examples; it requires neither teacher outputs nor intermediate solution traces. We select the student injection layer and intervention scale on a labeled support set and report results on the disjoint remainder of each evaluation split. On GSM8K and MATH, the projected vector improves base students by 10.37-21.98 accuracy points across the evaluated teacher-student settings. On four code-generation benchmarks, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student gains 3.23-4.67 pass@1 points, while the base Qwen2.5-7B student gains up to 9.65 points. These results show that a teacher-side reasoning vector can be reused across smaller students with different residual dimensions through projector-only adaptation.

items.title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?
items.description: arXiv:2611.34303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.

items.title: Learning from Unreliable Operator References: Claim-Level Rewards for Customer Support Agents
items.description: arXiv:2611.34341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even a correct operator reply can be an unreliable training target for a customer-support agent. About a quarter of the factual claims in these replies lacked full support in the agent's knowledge base and tool records. We treat operator replies as claims to verify rather than answers to imitate. Unverified claims guide revisions to the knowledge base and tools. Verified claims serve as coverage targets in a claim-level GRPO reward that scores factual precision against the evidence the agent retrieved for its answer. On an offline benchmark, 8.6% of the GRPO agent's text answers were flagged for hallucinations, compared with 13.6% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. In a randomized A/B test against the existing procedural bot, the deployed system increased the share of conversations closed without a human operator from 63.3% to 80.8%.

items.title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
items.description: arXiv:2611.34373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.

items.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2611.34427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.

items.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
items.description: arXiv:2611.34491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.

items.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.34492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.

items.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2611.34505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

items.title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
items.description: arXiv:2611.34529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

items.title: Technical Report MEG2text: Beyond Alignment in Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
items.description: arXiv:2611.34686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.

items.title: PoVi: Agentic Poetry-to-Video Generation with Knowledge Grounding and Figurative Understanding
items.description: arXiv:2611.34690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

items.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
items.description: arXiv:2611.34725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.

items.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
items.description: arXiv:2611.34776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

items.title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.34819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emotionally supportive interactions require large language models not only to avoid overtly harmful content, but also to recognize vulnerability-related risk, regulate their relational stance, preserve user agency, and provide context-appropriate support. Existing safety benchmarks often measure isolated violations, leaving unclear what underlying response competence their scores represent. We introduce VulnSafe, a Chinese capability assessment centered on Vulnerability-Aware Response Competence (VARC). VARC organizes relational safety into five complementary constructs: Risk Perception, Safety Preservation, Autonomy Protection, Supportive Response, and Boundary Management. Following an evidence-centered design, 41 scenarios elicit construct-relevant behavior through 2,050 balanced prompts and scenario-specific scoring rubrics. The assessment further separates proactive should-do behavior from prohibitive should-not behavior. Across eight representative LLMs, results show distinct competence profiles and larger disparities than prohibitive requirements. VulnSafe therefore makes relational safety interpretable as a multidimensional model capability rather than as refusal compliance alone.

items.title: The Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark: Do Language Models Know the Foundations of Early-Grade Literacy?
items.description: arXiv:2611.34823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many languages of instruction in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are poorly represented in the data used to train language models. Before these models can support early-grade literacy in such languages, we need to know whether they hold the linguistic knowledge of each language that literacy teaching relies on. To test this, we present the Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark and the reproducible, largely automated pipeline that turns curriculum documents, teacher guides and pupil books into a vetted question set organised on a fixed grid of nine linguistic domains and seven grade levels. The pipeline combines LLM-driven source survey, feature consolidation, item generation and quality control with an item-selection step inspired by item response theory and a final expert review. We instantiate it for Kiswahili (Kenya; 135 items) and English (United Kingdom; 137 items) and evaluate 121 and 119 models respectively. Frontier models exceed 90% accuracy in both languages, but accuracy falls steeply for smaller and cheaper models, and more so in Kiswahili. The two best models under 10 billion parameters reach 91.7% and 73.0% in English but only 51.9% and 40.7% in Kiswahili, and the mean accuracy of models deployable on mobile and tablet hardware is 47% in English against 24% in Kiswahili. The models most practical for low-resource classrooms are therefore the least capable in the languages they would serve. We release a 20-item sample per language, all pipeline prompts, open-source code, and a public leaderboard. This is the first rung of a three-level evaluation ladder for measuring and generating decodable text to support foundational literacy.

items.title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
items.description: arXiv:2611.34832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.

items.title: Tokenisation is not in APX
items.description: arXiv:2611.34938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

items.title: Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach
items.description: arXiv:2611.34092v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.

items.title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
items.description: arXiv:2611.34363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql

items.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
items.description: arXiv:2611.34397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.

items.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
items.description: arXiv:2611.34402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.

items.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
items.description: arXiv:2611.34420v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

items.title: Neural Rendering Compiler: Generative Video Models as Programmable Renderers
items.description: arXiv:2611.34680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.

items.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
items.description: arXiv:2611.34923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

items.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
items.description: arXiv:2611.34935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

items.title: AIで求人業務を効率化する方法10選！採用担当の工数を減らす進め方
items.description: 求人票の作成、応募者への返信、面接の日程調整に追われ、候補者と向き合う時間が取れない。他業務と兼務で採用を担う担当者ほど、この悩みを抱えやすいでしょう。 求人業務のうちAIに任せられる工程は、求人票の作成から採用データの分析まで10あります。なかでも 選考判断の前後にある連絡や記録の作業 から任せると、工数が減りやすくなります。 返信や日程調整が遅れるほど、候補者は先に連絡をくれた他社へ流れます。定型作業をAIに渡せば、面接や候補者の口説きに時間を回せます。 本記事では、工程別のAI活用法10選と、着手する工程を決めて効果を測るまでの5ステップを中心に解説します。 読み終える頃には、自社で最初にAIに任せる工程と、成果を上司に報告するための指標を決められるようになります。 AIで求人業務を効率化できる工程10選 求人業務のうち、AIで効率化できる工程は以下の10個です。 求人票の作成 媒体別の原稿展開 スカウト文面の作成 応募者からの問い合わせ対応 書類選考の一次確認 面接の日程調整 面接の記録と要約 評価シートと面接質問の作成 合否連絡と内定者フォロー 採用データの集計と分析 各工程でAIが担う作業と人が担う作業を分けて押さえると、任せすぎによる失敗を防げます。 求人票の作成 求人票は、 募集要件のメモからAIに初稿を書かせる ことで作成時間を短縮できます。白紙から文章を組み立てる時間が、もっとも工数を使う部分だからです。 たとえば職種名、業務内容、必須スキル、給与、勤務地を箇条書きで渡せば、ChatGPTやGeminiが求人票の形式に整えます。過去に応募が多かった求人票を参考として渡すと、自社らしい表現に近づきます。 一方、給与や労働条件の正確さ、仕事の魅力の打ち出し方は人が確認します。初稿づくりをAIに任せる分、現場社員へのヒアリングに時間を使えば、応募者に響く求人票に仕上げられます。 媒体別の原稿展開 1本の求人票をもとに、 媒体ごとの文字数や形式に合わせた原稿 をAIで書き分けられます。複数の求人媒体や自社採用サイトに掲載する企業ほど、書き直しの手間が積み上がるためです。 たとえば「キャッチコピーは30文字以内」「仕事内容は400文字以内」のように媒体の制約を指示すれば、AIが要約や言い換えをします。SNS向けの短い告知文も、同じ元原稿から作れます。 人が担うのは、書き分けた原稿で条件が食い違っていないかの確認です。元原稿を1本に絞って管理すれば、条件変更の反映漏れも防げます。 スカウト文面の作成 スカウトメールは、 候補者のプロフィールに合わせた個別文面 をAIに下書きさせると効率化できます。定型文の一斉送信では返信率が上がらず、1通ずつ書くと時間が足りないためです。 候補者の職務経歴の要点と自社求人の特徴を渡し、「経歴のどこに注目したかを冒頭で伝える」と指示すれば、AIが個別の書き出しを作ります。スカウト機能にAIを組み込んだ求人媒体や採用管理システムもあります。 送信する候補者の選定と、文面が経歴を誤って解釈していないかの確認は人が行います。下書きの時間が減れば、同じ時間で送れるスカウトの数を増やせます。 応募者からの問い合わせ対応 選考の流れや勤務条件に関する問い合わせは、 AIチャットボットで一次回答 できます。応募者の質問の多くは、求人票や採用サイトに答えがある定型的な内容だからです。 たとえば「リモート勤務は可能か」「選考は何回あるか」といった質問に、チャットボットが夜間や休日も自動で答えます。回答できない質問だけを担当者に引き継ぐ設定にすれば、担当者が対応する件数を絞れます。 人が担うのは、回答の元になるFAQの整備と、個別事情を含む相談への対応です。応募者を待たせない体制は、応募の取りこぼしを減らすことにもつながります。 書類選考の一次確認 書類選考では、 必須要件を満たしているかの照合と経歴の要約 をAIに任せられます。履歴書と職務経歴書を1通ずつ読み込む作業は、応募数に比例して時間が増えるためです。 たとえば「法人営業の経験3年以上」「普通自動車免許」といった要件を渡すと、AIが該当箇所を抜き出して一覧にします。担当者は要約を読んでから、気になる応募者の書類だけを詳しく確認できます。 ただし、合否の判断はAIに任せきりにせず人が行います。AIの照合結果を判断材料として使えば、確認の速さと判断の納得感を両立できます。 面接の日程調整 面接の日程調整は、 日程調整ツールとAIの組み合わせで自動化 しやすい工程です。候補日の提示、面接官の空き確認、確定連絡というやり取りの往復が、担当者の時間を細かく奪うためです。 面接官のカレンダーと連携した日程調整ツールを使えば、応募者が空き枠から希望日時を選ぶだけで予約が確定します。AIは日程変更の依頼メールを読み取り、返信文を下書きする役割を担えます。 人が担うのは、面接官の調整がつかない場合の個別対応です。応募から面接までの日数が縮まれば、候補者の志望度が高いうちに会えます。 面接の記録と要約 面接の内容は、 文字起こしと要約をAIに任せる ことで記録の手間を減らせます。面接中のメモ取りと面接後の清書は、面接官と担当者の双方に負担がかかるためです。 オンライン面接の録画や録音をAIで文字起こしし、「志望動機」「強み」「懸念点」の項目ごとに要約させれば、社内共有用の記録ができます。面接官はメモ取りから解放され、候補者との対話に集中できます。 録音や録画をする場合は、事前に候補者の同意を取ることが前提です。記録の質がそろえば、次の選考に進む面接官への引き継ぎもスムーズになります。 評価シートと面接質問の作成 評価シートと面接質問は、 求める人物像からAIに案を出させる と短時間で用意できます。職種ごとにゼロから評価項目を考えるのは、採用担当者にとって負担が大きい作業です。 たとえば「顧客折衝力」「チームでの課題解決」といった評価軸を渡すと、AIが評価基準と、それを確かめる行動事実の質問例を作ります。面接官ごとに質問がばらつく問題も抑えられます。 質問案のうち、職務と関係のない家族構成や出身地などを尋ねる内容が混ざっていないかは人が確認します。公正な選考の土台を整えることは、採用の質を保つことに直結します。 合否連絡と内定者フォロー 合否連絡や内定者へのフォローメールは、 AIで下書きを作って送信漏れを防ぐ ことで効率化できます。選考段階ごとに文面を書き分ける作業は、応募者が増えるほど遅れの原因になるためです。 不合格通知は応募者への配慮を保った定型文を、内定者フォローは入社までの手続きや懇親会の案内を、それぞれAIで作れます。採用管理システムと連携すれば、選考ステータスの変更に合わせて送信できます。 内定辞退の兆候がある候補者への連絡は、人が直接行います。定型連絡をAIに任せた分、内定者一人ひとりとの面談に時間を割けます。 採用データの集計と分析 媒体別の応募数や選考通過率は、 AIに集計と傾向の読み取りを任せられます 。表計算ソフトで手作業で集計していると、分析の前に時間切れになりやすいためです。 採用管理システムから書き出したCSVをChatGPTなどに読み込ませ、「媒体別の応募から内定までの通過率を出して」と指示すれば、集計表とグラフができます。どの媒体に予算を寄せるべきかを考える材料になります。 応募者の氏名などの個人情報は、読み込ませる前に削除します。データにもとづく改善が回り始めると、採用活動全体の精度が上がります。 求人業務で時間を奪っているのは判断の前後にある作業 採用担当者の時間を奪っているのは、合否の判断そのものではなく、その前後に発生する以下の3つの作業です。 日程調整と連絡の往復 面接後の記録と共有 社内の合否判断と条件調整 この3つの作業の実態を知ると、AIに最初に任せるべき工程が見えてきます。 日程調整と連絡の往復 日程調整は、 作業を分けて数えると想定より時間がかかる 工程です。1回ごとの作業は短くても、候補日の提示から確定連絡まで複数のやり取りが重なるためです。 株式会社ゼクウが採用担当者・人事責任者1,002名に実施した調査では、応募者1名への対応時間をまとめて尋ねた場合の中央値は約10分でした。一方、日程調整を候補日提示、面接官の空き確認、変更対応、確定連絡に分けて尋ねると、中央値は約14分でした。 出典： 採用業務の「見えない工数」実態調査2026（日本の人事部） 担当者の感覚よりも、細かな作業の積み重ねが工数を押し上げています。日程調整を自動化の候補に挙げれば、見えにくかった時間を取り戻せます。 面接後の記録と共有 面接後の記録と共有も、 選考判断の後ろで工数を生む作業 です。面接の内容を清書し、関係者に共有して評価をそろえるまでに、面接そのものとは別の時間がかかります。 前述のゼクウの調査でも、時間がかかる工程として面談後の記録、日程調整、連絡の往復が上位に挙がっています。また、HeaR株式会社は中途採用の書類選考を7工程・55タスクに分解し、合否を決める意思決定は1タスクのみで、連絡が19タスクを占めると公表しています。 出典： 書類選考55タスク分解レポート（HeaR株式会社） 判断以外の作業は手順が決まっているため、AIに任せやすい領域です。記録と共有を効率化すれば、面接官の負担も同時に軽くできます。 社内の合否判断と条件調整 選考が滞る最大の原因は、 社内の合否判断と条件調整 です。面接官や配属部署の確認待ちが発生すると、担当者が催促と再調整に追われます。 ゼクウの調査では、選考が滞る原因として「社内の合否判断・条件調整」が40.2%で最多、「日程調整」が37.3%で続きました。 出典： 採用業務の「見えない工数」実態調査2026（日本の人事部） 判断そのものは人が行いますが、AIは面接記録の要約や候補者の比較表を作り、判断材料をそろえる役割を担えます。判断に必要な情報が一目でわかれば、確認待ちの時間を縮められます。 AIで求人業務を効率化する4つのメリット AIで求人業務を効率化するメリットは、以下の4つです。 定型作業の工数を減らせる 応募から内定までの期間を短縮できる 担当者による品質のばらつきを抑えられる 夜間や休日も応募者に対応できる メリットを具体的に言語化しておくと、社内でAI導入の合意を得やすくなります。 定型作業の工数を減らせる AI活用の最大のメリットは、 手順が決まった作業の時間を減らせる ことです。求人票の初稿、連絡メール、面接記録の清書は、毎回同じ手順を繰り返す作業だからです。 たとえば合否連絡のメールを選考段階ごとにテンプレート化し、AIで候補者名や日程を差し込めば、1通ずつ文面を考える必要がなくなります。兼務の担当者ほど、細切れの作業が減る効果を実感しやすいでしょう。 浮いた時間は、候補者との面談や現場とのすり合わせに回せます。採用担当者が本来の役割である候補者の見極めと口説きに集中できる状態をつくれます。 応募から内定までの期間を短縮できる AIを使うと、 応募から内定までの各段階の待ち時間 を縮められます。書類確認や日程調整の遅れが、選考全体の期間を延ばす原因になっているためです。 書類選考の要約をAIが当日中に作り、面接日程を応募者が自分で予約できる状態にすれば、応募から一次面接までの日数が縮まります。複数社を並行して受ける候補者にとって、早い連絡は企業を選ぶ判断材料の1つです。 選考期間が短くなれば、他社に先を越されて辞退される機会も減ります。採用競争が激しい職種ほど、スピードの差が採用成果の差として表れます。 担当者による品質のばらつきを抑えられる AIを使うと、 求人票や面接評価の品質を一定にそろえやすく なります。同じ指示文やテンプレートを使えば、担当者が変わっても出力の形式と項目が統一されるためです。 たとえば求人票作成用の指示文に「仕事内容」「必須スキル」「歓迎スキル」「労働条件」の項目を固定しておけば、記載漏れが起きにくくなります。面接の評価シートも、評価軸と基準をAIで整えると面接官ごとの差が縮まります。 品質がそろうと、特定の担当者に業務が依存する属人化も解消に向かいます。異動や退職があっても採用の質を保てる体制は、組織にとって大きな安心材料です。 夜間や休日も応募者に対応できる AIチャットボットを使えば、 担当者の勤務時間外も応募者に対応 できます。在職中の転職希望者は、仕事を終えた夜間や休日に求人を探して応募することが多いためです。 夜間に届いた問い合わせにチャットボットが即座に答え、そのまま面接予約まで案内すれば、翌営業日まで応募者を待たせずに済みます。担当者は出勤後に、AIが対応しきれなかった案件だけを確認します。 応募者が関心を持った瞬間に応答できる体制は、応募意欲が冷める前に選考へ進んでもらうことにつながります。担当者の残業を増やさずに対応時間を広げられる点も、兼務の担当者には大きな利点です。 AIで求人業務を効率化する5ステップ AIで求人業務を効率化するには、以下の5ステップで進めます。 採用工程ごとの工数を棚卸しする 最初にAIに任せる工程を決める 工程に合ったツールを選ぶ 1職種・1工程で小さく試す 効果を測ってほかの工程に広げる いきなりツールを導入すると、工数が減らない工程にAIを入れてしまう失敗が起こります。 ステップ1：採用工程ごとの工数を棚卸しする 最初に、 採用工程ごとに1か月あたりの作業時間を書き出します 。どこに時間がかかっているかを把握しないと、効果の大きい工程を選べないためです。 前述の10工程を表の行に並べ、「1件あたりの作業時間」と「月の件数」を記入して掛け合わせます。日程調整のように細かな作業が重なる工程は、候補日の提示、面接官の空き確認、確定連絡のように作業を分けて記録すると実態に近づきます。 1〜2週間ほど実際の作業時間を記録すると、より正確な数値になります。棚卸しの結果は、導入後の効果を比べる基準値としてそのまま使えます。 ステップ2：最初にAIに任せる工程を決める 最初にAIに任せる工程は、 工数が大きく、手順が決まっていて、合否の判断を含まない工程 から選びます。この3条件を満たす工程は、AIに任せても失敗したときの影響が小さく、効果も見えやすいた

items.description: 発表資料やプレスリリースの締め切りが重なり、原稿をゼロから書く時間が足りないと感じている方は多いでしょう。ChatGPTに頼んでみたものの、硬い文章しか出てこず書き直した経験がある方もいるのではないでしょうか。 AIで原稿を作るときは、目的・読み手・素材を渡し、本文より先に構成を作らせると、手直しの少ない下書きが得られます。 「原稿を書いて」と頼むだけでは、誰にでも当てはまる一般的な文章になり、書き直しの手間は減りません。誤情報や他者の表現に似た文章をそのまま社外に出せば、会社の信用にも関わります。 本記事では、AIで原稿を作る5つの手順と、プレゼン・スピーチ・求人など原稿の種類別のプロンプト例を中心に解説します。 読み終えたときには、自分の原稿に合った指示で下書きを作り、事実確認まで済ませて提出できる状態になっています。ぜひ最後までご覧ください。 AIで原稿を作成する5ステップ AIで原稿を作成する手順は、以下の5ステップです。 原稿の目的と読み手を決める AIに渡す素材を集める 構成案を先に作らせる 構成に沿って本文を生成する 事実確認と自分の言葉で仕上げる 本文を書かせる前の準備と、生成後の仕上げに手間をかけるほど、書き直しの量は減ります。 ステップ1：原稿の目的と読み手を決める 最初に、 原稿の目的・読み手・分量の3点を言葉にしておきます 。AIは指示にない情報を一般論で補うため、この3点が曖昧だと誰にでも当てはまる文章になるからです。 目的は「新サービスへの問い合わせを増やす」「新入社員の不安を和らげる」のように、読み手にとってほしい行動まで書きます。読み手は役職や知識レベルまで具体的にするほど、言葉選びが合ってきます。 分量は、読む原稿なら文字数、話す原稿なら持ち時間で決めます。プレゼンやスピーチは 話す時間を基準にする と、当日の時間超過を防げます。 この3点は、後のステップでプロンプトにそのまま貼り付けて使えます。最初に5分かけて整理しておくと、AIとのやり取りの往復回数が減ります。 ステップ2：AIに渡す素材を集める 次に、原稿の中身になる素材を集めます。 AIが知らない社内の事実や数値は、素材として渡さない限り原稿に入りません 。 集めておきたい素材は以下のとおりです。 伝えたい要点を書き出した箇条書きのメモ 発表に使うスライドや企画書 過去に書いた同じ種類の原稿 数値・日付・固有名詞などの確定情報 自分の体験や具体的なエピソード とくにエピソードは、AIが最も作れない部分です。素材が少ないまま生成すると、AIはもっともらしい架空の話で埋めることがあります。 ただし、未発表の情報や個人情報を含む素材は、入力してよいかを先に確認してください。入力ルールは後述の注意点で解説しています。 ステップ3：構成案を先に作らせる 素材がそろったら、本文ではなく 見出しや話の流れだけを先に出力させます 。構成の段階で直すほうが、本文を書き直すより手間が小さいからです。 指示は以下のように、ステップ1の3点と素材を渡したうえで、構成だけを求めます。 以下の条件で原稿の構成案を作成してください。本文はまだ書かないでください。 # 目的 【例：新サービスへの問い合わせを増やす】 # 読み手 【例：中小企業の総務担当者。AIの知識は少ない】 # 分量 【例：1,500字】 # 素材 【メモ・スライドの内容を貼り付け】 # 出力形式 見出しと、各見出しで伝える要点を1〜2行で示してください。 出てきた構成は、順番の入れ替えや不要な見出しの削除など、人が判断して整えます。 伝える順番を自分で決めておく と、本文の論理が崩れにくくなります。 ステップ4：構成に沿って本文を生成する 整えた構成を渡し、本文を生成させます。 長い原稿は見出しごとに分けて生成する と、内容の薄い段落や途中での話の脱線が減ります。 本文を頼む際は、文体と避けたい表現もあわせて指定します。たとえば「ですます調」「1文は60字以内」「専門用語には説明を添える」などです。 先ほどの構成のうち、見出し1の本文を書いてください。 # 条件 ・文体：ですます調 ・1文は60字以内 ・専門用語には短い説明を添える ・素材にない数値や事例は書かず、必要な箇所は【要確認】と記載する 最後の条件のように、素材にない情報を書かせない指示を入れておくと、確認すべき箇所が一目でわかります。仕上げの作業が楽になる指示です。 ステップ5：事実確認と自分の言葉で仕上げる 生成された本文は下書きとして扱い、 事実確認と言い回しの修正を人が行って完成させます 。AIの文章には事実と異なる内容や、AI特有の言い回しが残るからです。 事実確認では、数値・日付・固有名詞・引用を、公式発表などの一次情報と1件ずつ照合します。そのうえで、以下の観点でAIくささを消していきます。 チェック項目 直し方 同じ語尾が3文以上続いている 体言を主語にする・文をつなげるなどで語尾を変える 「さまざまな」「重要です」など抽象的な言葉が多い 具体的な数値・名称・場面に置き換える 前置きや締めの一文が毎段落にある 結論から書き、繰り返しの締めを削る 自分の体験や社内の固有の話がない エピソードを1つ以上自分で足す 声に出すと詰まる箇所がある 音読して、言いにくい箇所を自分の話し方に直す とくにスピーチやプレゼンの原稿は、必ず一度声に出して読みます。耳で聞いて自然な文章に直すことで、自分の言葉として話せる原稿に仕上がります。 原稿の種類別AIプロンプト例7選 原稿の種類ごとにそのまま使えるプロンプト例を、以下の7つ紹介します。 プレゼン原稿 スピーチ原稿 記事・ブログ原稿 プレスリリース 求人原稿 社内報・メルマガ 動画台本 原稿の種類によって指定すべき項目は変わるため、自分が書く原稿の例から読み進めてください。 【プレゼン原稿】スライドから発表原稿を作る プレゼン原稿は、 スライドの内容と持ち時間を渡し、スライドごとに区切って出力させる のがポイントです。区切っておくと、発表中にどのスライドで何を話すかが迷わずわかります。 あなたは社内プレゼンの原稿作成を支援するアシスタントです。 以下のスライド内容をもとに、話し言葉の発表原稿を作成してください。 # 発表の目的 【例：来期の予算増額を承認してもらう】 # 聞き手 【例：経営層5名】 # 持ち時間 【例：10分】 # スライド内容 【スライド1〜10のテキストを貼り付け】 # 条件 ・スライドごとに見出しを付けて区切る ・話し言葉のですます調 ・スライドに書いてある文をそのまま読み上げる構成にしない 最後の条件を入れると、スライドの文字を読み上げるだけの原稿になるのを防げます。スライドに書けなかった背景や根拠を話す原稿になり、聞き手の納得感が高まります。 【スピーチ原稿】朝礼や式典の挨拶を作る スピーチ原稿では、 自分で用意したエピソードを必ず素材に入れます 。エピソードがないと、AIはどの会社でも使える一般的な挨拶を作ってしまうからです。 以下の条件で、スピーチ原稿を作成してください。 # 場面 【例：入社式での部長挨拶】 # 聞き手 【例：新入社員30名】 # 持ち時間 【例：3分】 # 伝えたいこと 【例：失敗を恐れず質問してほしい】 # 入れたいエピソード 【例：自分が新人時代に質問できず、納期を1週間遅らせた経験】 # 条件 ・話し言葉で、聞き手に語りかける口調 ・冒頭30秒でエピソードに入る ・最後は聞き手への期待で締める 朝礼・送別会・表彰式など場面が変わっても、場面と伝えたいことを差し替えるだけで使えます。 話し手の体験が入った原稿 は、聞き手の記憶に残りやすくなります。 【記事・ブログ原稿】オウンドメディアの記事を作る 記事・ブログ原稿は、 構成の作成と本文の作成を2回に分けて依頼します 。1回で全文を書かせると、見出し同士で内容が重なったり、後半の情報が薄くなったりしやすいからです。 オウンドメディアに掲載する記事の構成案を作成してください。 # テーマ 【例：中小企業がクラウド会計を選ぶポイント】 # 想定読者 【例：従業員30名以下の企業の経理担当者】 # 読者の悩み 【例：ツールが多く、どれを選べばよいかわからない】 # 文字数 【例：4,000字】 # 条件 ・見出しはH2とH3で構成する ・各見出しで伝える要点を1行で添える 構成を確認・修正したら、ステップ4のプロンプトで見出しごとに本文を生成します。読者の悩みを書いておくと、悩みの解決から逆算した構成が出てきます。 【プレスリリース】新サービスの発表文を作る プレスリリースは、 5W1Hと数値を素材として渡し、リリースの型で出力させます 。記者が必要な情報を探しやすい型に沿うことで、記事化の判断材料をそろえられるからです。 以下の情報をもとに、プレスリリースの原稿を作成してください。 # 発表内容（5W1H） ・誰が：【社名】 ・何を：【サービス名と概要】 ・いつ：【提供開始日】 ・どこで：【提供地域・チャネル】 ・なぜ：【開発の背景となる課題】 ・どのように：【提供方法・料金】 # 数値情報 【例：導入テストでの成果、価格など】 # 代表者コメント 【箇条書きで要点を記載】 # 出力形式 タイトル、リード文、本文、会社概要の順で作成してください。 素材にない数値は書かないでください。 代表者コメントは、AIに作らせた文章をそのまま載せず、本人に確認を取ってください。 素材にない数値を書かせない指示 を入れておくと、誤った数字が社外に出るリスクを抑えられます。 【求人原稿】募集職種の紹介文を作る 求人原稿は、仕事内容と働く魅力を渡したうえで、 法令で求められる明示事項が抜けていないかを人が確認します 。AIは法改正を反映していない場合があるからです。 以下の情報をもとに、求人サイトに掲載する求人原稿を作成してください。 # 職種 【例：法人営業】 # 仕事内容 【1日の流れ、担当する顧客、使うツールなど】 # 応募条件 【必須条件・歓迎条件】 # 働き方・待遇 【勤務地、勤務時間、給与、休日】 # この仕事の魅力 【現場社員の声など】 # 条件 ・求職者が入社後の1日を想像できる書き方にする ・性別や年齢を限定する表現は使わない 2024年4月から、募集時に「従事すべき業務の変更の範囲」「就業の場所の変更の範囲」なども明示が必要になりました。生成後に、明示事項がそろっているかを確認してください。 出典： 令和６年４月より、募集時等に明示すべき事項が追加されます（厚生労働省） 【社内報・メルマガ】社内外へのお知らせを作る 社内報やメルマガは、 伝えたい事実と読み手の関心をセットで渡す のがポイントです。事実だけを渡すと、読み手にとっての意味が書かれない事務連絡のような文章になるからです。 以下の内容で、社内報の記事を作成してください。 # 伝えたい事実 【例：4月から経費精算システムが新しくなる】 # 読み手 【例：全社員。毎月の経費精算に手間を感じている】 # 読み手にとってのメリット 【例：スマホで領収書を撮影するだけで申請できる】 # トーン 【例：親しみやすく、ですます調】 # 文字数 【例：600字】 # 条件 ・冒頭で読み手のメリットを伝える ・手続きの期限と問い合わせ先を最後に記載する メルマガの場合は、件名の案を5つほど同時に出させると、開封されやすい件名を選べます。冒頭で読み手のメリットを伝える構成にすると、最後まで読まれやすくなります。 【動画台本】ナレーション原稿を作る 動画台本は、 ナレーションとテロップを分けて出力させます 。耳で聞く言葉と画面で読む言葉は、適した長さや言い回しが違うからです。 以下の条件で、動画の台本を作成してください。 # 動画の目的 【例：新サービスの使い方を紹介する】 # 視聴者 【例：サービスを申し込んだばかりの担当者】 # 尺 【例：2分】 # 映像の流れ 【例：ログイン画面→初期設定→レポート画面】 # 出力形式 表形式で「時間」「映像」「ナレーション」「テロップ」の4列に分けてください。 表形式で出力させると、撮影や編集の担当者とそのまま共有できます。完成した台本は、実際に声に出して尺に収まるかを確かめてから撮影に進んでください。 AI原稿の質を上げるプロンプトのコツ6つ AI原稿の質を上げるプロンプトのコツは、以下の6つです。 AIに役割を与える 読み手と目的を具体的に書く 文字数や話す時間を指定する お手本の文章を渡す 使わない表現を指定する 対話で修正を重ねる プロンプト例を自分用に調整するときの判断基準として活用してください。 AIに役割を与える プロンプトの冒頭で 「あなたは〇〇の担当者です」と役割を与える と、原稿の視点と言葉選びがそろいます。役割に合わせて、AIが想定する読み手や専門用語の扱いが変わるからです。 たとえば同じ新サービスの紹介でも、「広報担当者」なら社外向けの客観的な文章になります。「営業担当者」なら顧客の課題に寄り添う提案調の文章になります。 役割は「BtoB企業で10年働く広報担当者」のように、経験や業界まで加えるとより具体的になります。原稿の種類に合った役割を選ぶことで、書き直す前の段階から自社らしい文章に近づきます。 読み手と目的を具体的に書く 読み手と目的は、 1文で具体的に書く ほど原稿の精度が上がります。読み手が曖昧なまま生成すると、AIは最も一般的な読み手を想定するからです。 曖昧な指定 具体的な指定 社員向けに 入社3年目までの営業担当者向けに サービスを紹介して 無料トライアルへの申し込みを促して わかりやすく AIを使ったことがない人にもわかるように 目的には、読み終えた人にとってほしい行動まで含めます。行動が決まると、AIは結論や締めの一文をその行動に向けて書くようになります。 文字数や話す時間を指定する 原稿の分量は、 文字数か話す時間で必ず指定します 。指定がないと、AIは用途に対して長すぎる、または短すぎる原稿を出すことがあるからです。 ただし、AIは指定した文字数をぴったり守るのが得意ではありません。生成後に文字数カウントで確認し、ずれていれば「あと300字短くして」のように調整を頼みます。 話す原稿は、自分の話す速さ
