In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

items.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.25594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

items.title: Social sycophancy differs across access modes of large language models
items.description: arXiv:2611.28012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

items.title: Grammar-as-a-Drafter: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
items.description: arXiv:2611.28349v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regular expressions, tool-call formats), the drafter works against a constraint it does not know, so its proposals for keys, delimiters, and indentation are often rejected or invalid, even though the grammar engine already knows the next tokens. We present Grammar-as-a-Drafter (GaaD), which makes the grammar a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens (out-degree 1 in the grammar automaton) into one draft row of width $K$ (which can exceed the drafter's proposal length $K_M$): matching tokens are promoted to GRAMMAR, the proposal is truncated where it disagrees, and grammar tokens fill the remaining slots. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter without adding kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, accepting canonical GRAMMAR drafts with probability 1 preserves grammar validity but can shift the output distribution relative to grammar-masked decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, and evaluate it on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP (Qwen3.5-0.8B; 1.99 to 5.31 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 for DFlash, and 1.30 to 3.64 for n-gram (Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x faster at batch size 64. In the Rust runtime, MTP with GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (1.22-1.69x at high concurrency). Under mixed traffic, GaaD finishes workloads 1.03-1.23x sooner while modestly raising plain-text TPOT.

items.title: Seeing vs. Knowing: Counterfactual Supervision and Correction for 3D-Aware Object Editing
items.description: arXiv:2611.29542v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.

items.title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
items.description: arXiv:2611.30235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

items.title: De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns
items.description: arXiv:2611.30509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.

items.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
items.description: arXiv:2611.30555v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

items.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
items.description: arXiv:2611.30986v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

items.title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis
items.description: arXiv:2611.33167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader's perspective.

items.title: Temporal Exposure to Byzantine Vulnerability Under Intermittent Participation in Federated Learning
items.description: arXiv:2611.33168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the effect of participation variability on per-round Byzantine vulnerability. We formalise Dynamic Participation Exposure (DPE), a phenomenon in which the global Byzantine fraction remains below an aggregation rule's tolerance threshold, while a participating client set violates, or approaches violation of, the assumptions required for robust aggregation. Under stochastic participation, we derive the probability of per round exposure and analyse how active-set size affects the variability of the observed Byzantine fraction. We further examine the accumulation of exposure over multiple rounds and consider adversaries that selectively participate during favourable rounds. Our analysis shows that intermittent participation does not automatically imply aggregation failure. Rather, it transforms Byzantine robustness from a static population-level property into a stochastic and temporal property. To mitigate this risk, we outline actionable design recommendations based on minimum active-set constraints, temporal monitoring, participation history, and adaptive aggregation.

items.title: Geophysics-informed invertible operator network for Bayesian geophysical inversion
items.description: arXiv:2611.33178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geophysical inverse problems are inherently ill-posed because of sparse observations and measurement noise. Classical sampling-based Bayesian inference methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), are computationally prohibitive because they require many forward simulations. Data-driven machine-learning methods often struggle to produce physically consistent solutions when training data are limited. To address these issues, we propose a geophysics-informed invertible operator network (GI-ION) that integrates an invertible neural network (INN) within a deep operator-learning framework for efficient Bayesian geophysical inversion. The INN serves as the branch network and transforms the model parameters into branch coefficients that represent the forward solution and a latent variable that captures uncertainty in the inverse problem. By learning the forward operator and enforcing statistical independence between the branch coefficients and the latent variable, GI-ION enables efficient sampling from a learned conditional approximation, even with sparse boundary observations. We validated GI-ION on three representative cases: 1D surface-wave dispersion and travel-time tomography for a 2D synthetic random-field model and a seismic-slice model. Numerical experiments demonstrate robust performance across diverse problem settings and efficient conditional sampling.

items.title: Deep Learning-Based Mesoscopic Emission Modeling
items.description: arXiv:2611.33179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traffic-related emissions are a major contributor to urban air pollution. However, existing emission models face a fundamental trade-off: macroscopic models are computationally efficient but rely on average speeds, leading to systematic errors, while microscopic models achieve high accuracy but are computationally prohibitive for large scale simulations. To bridge this gap, this study introduces Direct Emission Prediction (DEP), a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based deep learning model. DEP was trained on over one million synthetic trips generated by coupling real-world GNSS speed profiles with the microscopic emission model MOBSim. By processing sequential link-level inputs, including vehicle characteristics, road attributes, and ambient temperature, DEP predicts CO$_2$ and NOx emissions. We integrated DEP into a MATSim-based workflow and applied it to the Ile-de-France region. DEP matches the accuracy of SPG-M, a hybrid mesoscopic-microscopic reference model, within 0.35% for CO$_2$ and 1.87% for NOx across both hot and cold-start scenarios, while reducing computational runtime to just 2.2%. Furthermore, validation against empirical remote sensing data confirms that DEP accurately reproduces real-world NOx emission levels across Euro 2-6 diesel vehicles, whereas traditional macroscopic tools like COPERT and HBEFA systematically underestimate them. Finally, DEP effectively captures the spatial distribution of cold-start emissions, identifying key hotspots in dense urban areas. This work demonstrates that deep learning-based mesoscopic frameworks can achieve microscopic accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling scalable, high-resolution urban emission modeling without relying on pre-computed emission factor databases.

items.title: Resource-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Early Rice Blast Forecasting in Sustainable Agriculture
items.description: arXiv:2611.33237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resource-efficient artificial intelligence has become increasingly important for sustainable agriculture, where timely disease forecasting must be achieved under computational and energy constraints. Early estimation of rice blast can enhance food security by optimizing crop management practices while reducing excessive pesticide use. However, existing frameworks often suffer from high computational overhead and limited capability to model the complex spectral-temporal dependencies present in heterogeneous meteorological and remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a lightweight multimodal fusion framework comprising an attentive positional encoding-based Transformer and a convolutional neural network (CNN)-embedded gated recurrent unit (GRU) for efficient spectral-temporal representation learning. The attention-enhanced positional encoding assigns adaptive importance to sequential meteorological tokens, enabling effective modelling of temporal characteristics. In parallel, the lightweight CNN extracts discriminative spectral features, while the GRU captures temporal dynamics from remote sensing imagery acquired over two time-instances. A multimodal fusion layer integrates these heterogeneous representations to forecast rice blast risk 5-10 days before symptom manifestation across diverse agro-climatic zones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a validation accuracy of 96.93% and an F1-score of 95.79%. In addition to its predictive performance, the lightweight multimodal architecture substantially reduces computational complexity, inference latency, and carbon emissions, making it an energy-efficient solution for large-scale disease forecasting. The proposed framework provides a practical foundation for resource-efficient artificial intelligence in sustainable agriculture.

items.title: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data
items.description: arXiv:2611.33248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The UCI Heart Disease data are a widely used machine-learning benchmark. We show that their chest-pain variable is stored in reverse of its documentation. At all four sites, the code documented as "asymptomatic" (4) marks patients with typical angina, and the code documented as "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of the classical angina features (at Cleveland, no chest pain). Two complementary checks establish this: (i) the chest-pain table and regression coefficients of the original 1986 Cleveland study are reproduced only under the corrected reading; (ii) in the Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach files, 93-96% of patients coded 4 have all three classical angina features. A 1990 word-labeled Cleveland file already uses the documented labels, and Statlog (Heart), a Cleveland subset, stores the same codes. OpenML, PMLB and two highly voted Kaggle copies that name the categories use the same documented labels (about 400,000 downloads combined). We audited a seeded random sample of 150 records from a pre-specified Scholar query for SHAP studies of these data mentioning asymptomatic chest pain (124 readable). Of 32 papers that state a direction for a named category, 25 (78%; 95% CI 61-89%) state one inconsistent with the corrected category identities; 22 (69%; 51-82%; post hoc) are attributable to the documentation error, and nine of these explain it clinically. None of the 124 readable papers identifies the reversal. Conventional models are essentially unaffected, one reason the error went unnoticed. Interpretations that attach the documented names to model effects are reversed, and zero-shot language-model classifiers that read the labels are misled: with the documented labels, three open-weight models lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) given age, sex and chest-pain type. We give the corrected mapping, evidence and code.

items.title: FERRETS: A Scalable Symbolic Transform for Time Series Classification
items.description: arXiv:2611.33249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dictionary methods for time series build bags of symbolic words from subsequences, but the accurate ones scale poorly. Against other families of methods, their accuracy no longer pays for their cost. We present FERRETS, a label-free dictionary transform built on WEASEL~2. It keys windows of random length and dilation into exact eight-bit words, adds a level word of each window's mean and spread, and on multivariate data adds cross-channel words. We compare it with leading classifiers, deep networks and foundation models included, on the UCR, Multiverse and MONSTER archives. FERRETS is the fastest of the eleven methods timed on UCR under a ten-thread budget. Of the ten others, only MultiRocket-Hydra is significantly more accurate, taking 24.7 times as long. FERRETS is not significantly different from WEASEL~2, the most accurate earlier dictionary method, which takes 125 times as long, and is significantly ahead of the other dictionary methods. On the Multiverse core, it is not significantly different in accuracy from HIVE-COTE~2 and MultiRocket-Hydra, though behind both on UCR. It is also significantly more accurate than five frozen foundation models on UCR's published split. On the MONSTER problems both complete, MiniRocket takes 3.7 times as long to fit as the streaming FERRETS classifier, which is significantly more accurate.

items.title: Change Partners at Every Layer: Balanced Random Regrouping for Model Merging
items.description: arXiv:2611.33308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.

items.title: Sparse Adaptation for In-Context Learning on Data Streams
items.description: arXiv:2611.33325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.

items.title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
items.description: arXiv:2611.33332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.

items.title: FlowersBench: A FluidFlower-Inspired Dataset for Benchmarking Carbon Storage Surrogates Across Geological Structures
items.description: arXiv:2611.33335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning surrogates are emerging as a computationally efficient tool for uncertainty quantification in geological carbon storage (GCS). Geological structure constitutes a major source of uncertainty; however, existing benchmark simulation datasets predominantly vary petrophysical and operational parameters within a fixed geological setting. Generalisation to unseen geological structures therefore remains largely unexplored. We introduce FlowersBench, a benchmark dataset of 5,000 two-dimensional, reservoir-scale CO$_2$ storage simulations across 244 structural geometries. The geometries are sampled from an in-house structural generator inspired by the FluidFlower experiments and Case B of the 11th Society of Petroleum Engineers Comparative Solution Project (SPE11B). Each simulation is run with Open Porous Media (OPM) Flow over a 50-year injection period and a 500-year post-injection monitoring period. Test geometries are withheld from training to assess generalisation to unseen structural geometries. Two additional subsets support evaluation under structural shift. The first extends the parameter ranges of the structural generator beyond those used for training, and the second introduces an unseen topology of multiple parallel faults. A baseline U-Net surrogate is trained to predict CO$_2$ gas saturation. In representative test cases, the surrogate recovers the main migration pathways, including lateral spreading beneath low-permeability layers and upward flow along fault damage zones, with errors concentrated near the plume boundary. Under both structural shifts, prediction error exceeds that on the held-out geometries, and the increase in relative error is greater for the unseen fault topology. FlowersBench is publicly available and provides a common basis for evaluating GCS surrogates across geological structures.

items.title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
items.description: arXiv:2611.33351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.

items.title: The Marauder's Map: B\'{e}zier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
items.description: arXiv:2611.33353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional B\'ezier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.

items.title: Discovering Explicit Magnetic Core-Loss Equations via Symbolic Sparse Identification
items.description: arXiv:2611.33364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact core loss equations are essential tools in magnetic component design, but existing approaches trade accuracy against interpretability. Empirical models such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) yield compact expressions of limited accuracy, while machine learning methods achieve high accuracy as black-box predictors. This paper bridges the gap with a Symbolic Sparse Identification (SSI) framework, which casts core loss modeling as a data-driven symbolic regression problem and recovers unknown equations directly from measured data, without presuming a functional form. First, a comprehensively expanded library of symbolic candidate terms far richer than the SE is constructed. Second, the governing terms are isolated from this library by sparse regression. Third, the coefficients of the retained terms are refined with an AdamW optimizer to maximize accuracy and form an analytical equation. Experiments on Fair-Rite 78, 79, and 95 yield test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56%, respectively, with only 10, 10, and 7 active terms. Comparisons with empirical, numerical, and symbolic models quantify the resulting balance of accuracy and compactness. SSI thus provides an explicit and physically guided approach for high-frequency magnetic characterization and design.

items.title: Federated Learning with Uncertainty Quantification on Pseudo Label Exchange
items.description: arXiv:2611.33395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate federated stochastic operator learning for stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), with an emphasis on heterogeneous client data distributions and uncertainty quantification. Federated learning enables clients to collaboratively train models without exchanging their original solution data, but conventional federated averaging can suffer significant performance degradation when client distributions differ, particularly when their input function supports are disjoint. To address these challenges, we propose the Federated Stochastic Operator Network (FedSON), a two-phase framework that combines auxiliary data construction with stochastic operator learning. In the first phase, locally trained deterministic neural operators and their corresponding input functions are exchanged to generate pseudolabeled auxiliary data, enabling the federated model to learn across heterogeneous input distributions without sharing original solution trajectories. In the second phase, a stochastic operator network is trained on top of the frozen deterministic operator to characterize stochastic fluctuations and quantify uncertainty in the predicted solutions. Numerical experiments involving the heat equation, viscous Burgers' equation, and two-dimensional advection-diffusion equation demonstrate the FedSON substantially improves deterministic prediction accuracy under heterogeneous client distributions while producing uncertainty estimates comparable to those obtained through centralized training.

items.title: Yet Another Concept Drift Benchmark? A Principled Framework for Evaluating Drift Detectors
items.description: arXiv:2611.33424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Concept drift detection is a fundamental component of data stream learning, yet its empirical evaluation remains based on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. We propose a principled benchmark grounded in an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics. Our framework introduces finite detection windows and repeated alarms, enabling a clear separation between detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, and employs a reproducible observer to provide a controlled and interpretable performance signal. Building on this formulation, we define normalized evaluation metrics and a composite score addressing limitations of existing measures. We validate the framework through a large-scale stress-testing evaluation of 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.

items.title: Scalpel and Brush: Pruning and Targeted Weight Editing of a Small Language Model by a Single LLM Agent
items.description: arXiv:2611.33426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It has recently been shown that an LLM can itself edit the weights of a language model, yet it remains unclear which part of such a result is due to the agent and which part is reproduced by a random edit of the same shape, by an instruction in the prompt, or by a standard procedure without an LLM. We unify repair and pruning as sparse weight edits to optimize a metric we specify, using BLEU as an example: three tasks -- targeted weight repair ("brush"), structured MLP neuron pruning ("scalpel", zeroing pruned weights), and layer removal with repair - are assigned to a DeepSeek Harness agent powered by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with up to 50 dev evaluations. We study Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct in three independent runs per task, with final evaluation on two hidden splits. On ordinary differential equations, changing at most 0.0084% of weights raised test BLEU by 24-32% on second-order equations and by a factor of 1.8-2.5 on equations with polynomial right-hand sides. An independent substitution check showed that higher BLEU reflects notation alignment rather than improved correctness. Masks that remove 12.5-15% of MLP neurons shrink the model by 9.4-11.2% with mean BLEU loss of at most 0.01 on both hidden splits, whereas standard pruning with equal shares per layer failed the constraint at all tested shares. On seven-class GoEmotions classification, edits raise macro-F1 from 0.100 to 0.396-0.451 on test and from 0.175 to 0.455-0.476 on holdout. A ridge-based classifier written into agent-selected weight rows yields macro-F1 of 0.424 and 0.464. Pruning search with the same evaluation limit removes 15.9% of neurons versus 14-21.4% for agent runs passing the hidden check. Standard procedures without an LLM reproduce much of the performance once given the location and form of intervention found by the agent; a comparison of agentic and non-agentic search remains open.

items.title: Fast Muscle-Driven Whole-Body Motion Tracking with a Differentiable World Model
items.description: arXiv:2611.33460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.

items.title: Differentially Private Policy Optimization in Linear MDPs with Adversarial Rewards
items.description: arXiv:2611.33469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in personalized services often relies on sensitive interaction data. Motivated by the need to protect these data, we study differentially private (DP) policy optimization in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback. This setting poses two key challenges: past trajectories are repeatedly reused for policy evaluation, and reward choices may depend on previously released private statistics. The proposed algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP). With all other parameters fixed, our high-probability regret bound retains the same leading $\widetilde{O}\left(K^{3/4}\right)$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$ as the corresponding non-private bound for batched optimistic PPO. The additional privacy terms scale as $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{5/8}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{1/2}\right)$. Thus, privacy incurs only lower-order additive costs in $K$, even under adaptive adversarial rewards.

items.title: Evaluation and Restoration of Safety in Reasoning-Tuned LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2611.33515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-source LLMs that are optimized for reasoning, such as VibeThinker, aim to democratize AI by bringing high-capability models to users with limited resources. They are broadly available but lack regulation and external guardrails; therefore, in order to integrate them safely into human society, it is critical that they perform in a safe manner. There are popular and intuitive arguments for why improved reasoning should improve safety, but recent evidence suggests that, in fact, the opposite may be true. This paper aims to characterize and mitigate this issue. First, it develops a metric for evaluating LLMs optimized for reasoning, and shows that increasing reasoning across multiple model families increases the unsafe rate in all cases. Second, it proposes a method for restoring safety by combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail (ESPG). Compared to alternative methods for safety post-training such as GRPO, ESPG is simple to implement, requires no GPU memory beyond that of inference, and works with remarkably few training samples (e.g.\ 30), yet makes the model significantly safer. The study thus establishes a path towards safe post-training of open-source AI models.

items.title: A Perturbation-Driven Framework for Sensitivity Analysis of Dimensionality Reduction
items.description: arXiv:2611.33523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-dimensional representations produced by dimensionality reduction (DR) are commonly evaluated using distortion measures such as trustworthiness and continuity. In this paper, we study the sensitivity of DR methods to plausible input variations by quantifying changes in structural preservation and visually diagnosing how these changes manifest in the resulting representations. This perspective reflects the fact that real-world datasets are finite, noisy samples of an underlying distribution, and DR should not produce substantially different structures under small data changes. We introduce a model-agnostic, perturbation-driven sensitivity evaluation framework that treats perturbations as controlled probes of plausible data variation. Across multiple perturbation families and strength levels, we repeatedly perturb the input, apply a DR method, and evaluate the resulting low-dimensional representations using a set of distortion measures to derive sensitivity profiles for each DR method. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through case studies on DR method comparison, behavior analysis, and robustness improvement. We find that methods performing well according to conventional distortion measures (e.g., t-SNE) can still exhibit substantial sensitivity, leading to instability in visually salient structures such as trajectories and clusters, while certain methods (e.g., multidimensional scaling) may exhibit improved structural preservation under specific perturbations. These results highlight the importance of sensitivity analysis for comparing DR methods, diagnosing perturbation-sensitive visual patterns, and guiding the development of more robust DR methods toward trustworthy visual analytics.

items.title: Deletion You Can Check: Auditing LLM Unlearning
items.description: arXiv:2611.33525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A common indication that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record is a membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC $\approx 0.5$). This reading is sound only if the comparison population represents how the record should behave after a valid deletion---a counterfactual that is rarely validated. We test this premise in a controlled $2\times2$ study pairing two membership-inference benchmarks, ArxivMIA and BookMIA, with two language models, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B. Exact retraining validates the membership reference: it lies within the prespecified chance band on ArxivMIA but reaches $0.122$ on BookMIA, causing the same metric to reject an empirical deletion reference. A post-hoc BookMIA/Qwen diagnostic replaces benchmark label-0 records with same-pool, never-fine-tuned records and moves the reference from $0.257$ to $0.523$, supporting population mismatch in that cell. Each approximate-unlearning checkpoint is judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift beyond non-deletion variation, and utility. On the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama axis, no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (GA+GD), negative-preference optimization with retain training (NPO-RT), or teacher--student unlearning (SCRUB) passes. A score near chance is not evidence of forgetting until a reference establishes what chance means.

items.title: Casper: A Projection-Based Neurosymbolic Layer for Scalable & Guaranteed Constraint Satisfaction
items.description: arXiv:2611.33527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many real-world problems demand exact constraint satisfaction to be meaningfully solved, yet existing neurosymbolic methods face a stark trade-off: those that guarantee satisfaction fail to scale, while those that scale must resort to approximation. Meanwhile, traditional deep learning approaches offer no satisfaction guarantees at all. In this paper, we propose Casper, a neurosymbolic layer that simultaneously (i) guarantees constraint satisfaction, (ii) scales at inference time, (iii) is fully automated, requiring no problem-specific engineering, and (iv) is fully differentiable, making it composable with any neural predictor both at training and at inference time. Casper casts constraint satisfaction as a closed-form Euclidean projection onto the constraint-feasible region, computable in a single forward pass. Experiments across MNIST arithmetic (up to 1024 digits), Sudoku solving, and Warcraft pathfinding show that Casper is the only method that produces guaranteed-valid outputs at scale: on $30\times30$ Warcraft grids, exact baselines time out and approximate ones produce valid paths less than 7% of the time, while Casper produces them 100% of the time.

items.title: DiffER$^2$: Diffusion Ensembles for Retrosynthesis Prediction with SMILES Adapted Particle Guidance
items.description: arXiv:2611.33557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational retrosynthesis prediction has the potential to reduce development time for newly discovered drugs by automatically generating potential reactions for a target product. Data-driven approaches commonly treat this as a sequence-to-sequence generation task on SMILES strings. In this work, we construct ensembles of discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models for molecular generation and incorporate guidance mechanisms for improved output diversity. We propose an adaptation of particle guidance to SMILES sequence generation which significantly improves the number of unique molecules generated by diffusion ensembles while increasing top-k accuracy. These results further expand the efficacy of discrete diffusion for SMILES generation, and our empirical analyses offer new insights into the capabilities of diffusion models for chemical retrosynthesis.

items.title: Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning for Backdoor Removal
items.description: arXiv:2611.33571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a severe threat to modern NLP models by embedding hidden triggers that induce malicious behavior at inference time. Recent unlearning methods such as gradient ascent (GA) attempt to remove backdoors by maximizing the loss on poisoned samples; however, these methods can suffer from a critical limitation: they may shift the trigger's influence to other classes rather than eliminating it. In this work, we propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), a framework for mitigating textual backdoor behavior by enforcing prediction and representation invariance to trigger insertion. TICU constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs, then fine-tunes the model so that both inputs produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations. To preserve clean-task performance, TICU also retains the supervised classification loss on clean data and constrains parameter drift from the original model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings show that TICU improves triggered accuracy and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts compared with existing baselines, while maintaining competitive label-flipping performance and limiting clean-task degradation.

items.title: Amortizing Exact Orthogonality: Drift-Triggered Restoration for Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
items.description: arXiv:2611.33589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $\tau$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $\tau^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $\tau=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.

items.title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
items.description: arXiv:2611.33645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.

items.title: The Danger of Double Precision: Working Precision as a Hidden Constraint in Gaussian Process Maximum Likelihood
items.description: arXiv:2611.33647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are routinely fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, although for smooth kernels and noiseless data the covariance matrix is often more ill conditioned than double precision can resolve. For a squared-exponential kernel on a design with a Bayesian-optimization cluster, refits over a range of significand widths, judged against a high-precision reference, show that the double-precision fit is a different model and that fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits. Cholesky failure acts as an implicit conditioning constraint, caused mostly by rounding of the kernel entries; the constrained solution predicted from the working precision alone is within 20% of the best Powell fits at five of the six precisions from 40 to 64 bits, with a local expansion proved for the idealized problem. Across 43 kernels, designs and problem settings, including negative controls that double precision already resolves, the bits needed follow the log condition number at the reference optimum plus a tolerance-dependent offset, and at the loosest tolerance double precision suffices for the Matern 1.5 kernel but not for the squared-exponential kernel on clustered designs. Double-precision hyperparameters overstate the posterior standard deviation near the design cluster and, on a quadratic objective whose likelihood heads to the flat limit, stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers the reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for a posterior bias.

items.title: PRIOR: Pre-Call Reasoning in SFT and Its Influence on Tool-Use Retention under RL
items.description: arXiv:2611.33648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.

items.title: Self-supervised Clipped-objective Reinforcement Leaning Framework for Risk-aware Portfolio Management
items.description: arXiv:2611.33652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portfolio management involves balancing diverse financial assets, a critical yet challenging task in quantitative trading. Although deep reinforcement learning has emerged as an active research domain for solving complex sequential decision-making problems over the past decade, deploying reinforcement learning frameworks in non-stationary financial markets raises formidable difficulties. Most existing reinforcement learning-based portfolio management models fail to account for tick-level intraday market dynamics (e.g., order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations), which reflect rapid capital movements. Simultaneously, these models suffer from unstable learning processes due to reinforcement learning's inherent high variance. This paper presents a Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (SCP), which addresses these limitations through a two-phase architecture. Market feature integration phase (application contribution) integrates micro-level market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators to enhance sensitivity to intraday asset trend dynamics. Policy optimization Phase (AI contribution) employs intermediate asset state representations to derive optimal portfolio allocations via a self-supervised clipped-objective policy-learner, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on three major index datasets from China's A-share market demonstrate that SCP's superior performance in balancing risk-return trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Exploratory and ablation studies further validate the contributions of SCP's key components.

items.title: Flipping the Coins: Training Physical Simulators through Hard Switches
items.description: arXiv:2611.33716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid simulators embed learnable components such as neural networks in physical solvers and train them on reference trajectories. Many scientific solvers feature hard switches, such as a tripping power line, an igniting grid cell, or depolarizing brain tissue, where the loss exhibits discrete jumps across switch flips, leaving standard automatic differentiation to capture only its smooth part. Existing training paradigms face a fundamentally challenging trade-off, as gradient-based relaxations smooth the switches and introduce bias across jumps, whereas derivative-free methods treat the solver as a black box and discard path gradients of the continuous dynamics. Here we introduce EventFlip, which flips a near-threshold switch from a stored state, replays the original solver, and measures the loss difference between the two runs, in effect a finite difference across the switch. By perturbing every threshold with small Gaussian noise, we cast each switch as a stochastic binary decision and derive an unbiased gradient estimator that combines the continuous path gradient with a jump term constructed from these counterfactual rollouts. EventFlip-Rand optimizes this noise-averaged objective, whereas EventFlip-Hard operates on the deterministic hard-switch simulator used at deployment and provably targets the complete discontinuous loss. Under an identical forward evaluation budget, we benchmark EventFlip against twelve baselines across a power-grid cascade, a detonation wave, and cortical spreading depolarization, achieving the lowest error on every task and reducing the strongest baseline's error by factors of 1.5, 1.4, and 1.4, respectively.

items.title: Understanding Mode Collapse in Diffusion Models under Classifier-Free Guidance
items.description: arXiv:2611.33719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of classifier-free guidance in diffusion and flow models has proven critical to their empirical success, as it allows for the controllable generation of lower-temperature and higher-fidelity samples. Despite its widespread use, classifier-free guidance remains both empirically and theoretically poorly understood, owing to the difficulty of solving the associated transport equations for arbitrary normalizing flows. In this paper, we observe that the effects of classifier-free guidance arise from a mismatch between the representation capabilities of the conditional and unconditional distributions, wherein the conditional distribution exhibits higher complexity and fidelity. We propose an analytical model to capture this observation: the conditional distribution is a Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid, and the unconditional distribution is a single Gaussian approximating the mixture. The flows arising from this mixture are closed under scaling, enabling us to derive analytic closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. Our analytic solution shows that classifier-free guidance induces (a) a shift along a mean-axis direction and (b) a persistent skew toward, and concentration around, a singular point corresponding to the conditional sample starting from zero noise. We validate our theoretical predictions on pretrained, large-scale image diffusion models.

items.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
items.description: arXiv:2611.33732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.

items.title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2611.33766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.

items.title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
items.description: arXiv:2611.33825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.

items.title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.33872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.

items.title: The Gradient Difference Induced by Detaching the Denominator in QK Normalization
items.description: arXiv:2611.33887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: QK normalization divides each query and key by its own RMS norm before the attention scores are computed. Treating this denominator as a constant during backpropagation leaves the forward pass unchanged but alters the parameter gradients. We derive a closed form for the difference between the gradient under this detached rule and the gradient under the standard rule. For a single token, this difference is parallel to the token's own query; it changes only the query norm and has no first-order effect after normalization. The queries, however, are computed by a projection matrix $W_Q$ shared across all tokens. The gradient difference on $W_Q$ therefore equals $W_Q$ right-multiplied by a weighted second moment of the inputs, and it decomposes exactly into three components: a radial component that changes only the norm of $W_Q$, a tangential component that changes the query directions of other tokens, and an upstream component that changes the gradient passed to earlier layers. Under AdamW, the radial component drives $W_Q$ to a larger equilibrium norm and reduces its angular update per step. Paired experiments on a small Transformer language model are consistent with this analysis. Detaching the query denominator consistently raises the test loss, and the gap persists across hardware, evaluation datasets and learning rates. All three components remain non-negligible throughout training, with the tangential component the largest. Norm growth and the smaller angular update appear only on the detached projection matrix, while the other projection matrix is essentially unchanged. With a learnable scale, however, we observe no resolvable loss gap.

items.title: On the Learnability of Model Reprogramming: A Reachability and Relabeling Perspective
items.description: arXiv:2611.33889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model reprogramming adapts a frozen source model to a target task by wrapping it in a learnable input transformation from target input to the source-model input space, and an output mapping from source-model outputs to target predictions. Despite extensive empirical progress, the finite-sample learnability of the induced wrapper hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ remains underexplored. We address this for source models that expose hard source labels and analyze it through the wrapper structure: on any target samples, the input transformation selects reachable source labels that the output mapping relabels. Through this lens, we answer two questions: (1) how many target samples are needed to approach the best predictor in $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$, and (2) what gap remains between the optimum over $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ and the target Bayes risk. For (1), the wrapper structure factorizes the sample-wise complexity of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ into a reachability term counting reachable source-label patterns, and a conditional relabeling term counting their relabelings. This yields an agnostic-PAC bound on the estimation error, with sample complexity scaling additively in the two terms; this bound becomes closed-form on additive input transformations and is matched by a lower bound on an explicit binary classification construction. For (2), the same structure decomposes the approximation error exactly into the source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction with a source-conditional upper bound on this gap. We extend the approximation analysis to logit-exposing source models, where the upper bound is empirically estimable. The wrapper-side analysis localizes both errors to specific components, giving a structural view of reprogramming practice.

items.title: CondUQ: Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification Using Distribution Matching
items.description: arXiv:2611.33939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many applications, especially reliability- and safety-critical ones, require accurate uncertainty quantification for the outputs of model- or learning-based measurement, estimation, and prediction systems. The errors of such systems often vary with factors such as input quality and operating conditions, and thus cannot be accurately described by a single Gaussian model. Although Gaussian mixture models and calibrated quantiles can approximate such error distributions, their unconditional forms do not capture how the error behavior depends on these factors. Hence, we propose condUQ, an approach that conditions error models on observable factors for enabling accurate and reliable uncertainty quantification. condUQ is built on top of an existing system without modifying it and applies even when the system is a black box. First, condUQ maps the observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors sharing the same QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian conditional distribution. The QI predictor is trained end-to-end with a distribution-matching objective, without requiring quality labels. Second, for each QI, a Gaussian error model is then fitted and calibrated on a large held-out dataset. condUQ is demonstrated on three examples: (a) GPS multipath errors conditioned on satellite elevation and signal strength, (b) relative attitude errors of a transformer-based visual relative pose regression model conditioned on its internal features of the image pairs, and (c) prediction errors of a world model conditioned on the input observations and actions. In all three examples, condUQ substantially reduces the discrepancy between the modeled and empirical error distributions compared with a single global model. Moreover, the learned QIs reveal how the underlying factors affect the error characteristics in a manner consistent with physical principles.

items.title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
items.description: arXiv:2611.33951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation.
