Multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) algorithms aim to strategically combine these information sources to achieve an optimal trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost. However, existing MFBO methods often oversimplify the complex dependencies between fidelity levels or rely on heuristic acquisition functions that lack theoretical performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we introduce a new formulation of the MFBO problem as a fused Gaussian Process bandit and develop a corresponding Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. Our approach accurately predicts the high-fidelity function by fusing multi-fidelity observations through an autoregressive Gaussian Process model and explicitly quantifies the uncertainty arising from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The proposed method also provides theoretical simple-regret guarantees, overcoming a key limitation of existing MFBO algorithms that lack provable performance bounds. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated via both theoretical analysis and empirical studies.

items.title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
items.description: arXiv:2611.33080v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
items.description: arXiv:2611.33102v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived (rather than freshly generated) rollouts, but this generally leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy we call maximum likelihood replay: fitting the model to its archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood replay on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

items.title: Dynamic Tensor Product Regression
items.description: arXiv:2210.03961v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we initiate the study of Dynamic Tensor Product Regression. One has matrices $A_1\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times d_1},\ldots,A_q\in \mathbb{R}^{n_q\times d_q}$ and a label vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\ldots n_q}$, and the goal is to solve the regression problem with the design matrix $A$ being the tensor product of the matrices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_q$ i.e. $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\ldots d_q}} \|(A_1\otimes \ldots\otimes A_q)x-b\|_2$. At each time step, one matrix $A_i$ receives a sparse change, and the goal is to maintain a sketch of the tensor product $A_1\otimes\ldots \otimes A_q$ so that the regression solution can be updated quickly. Recomputing the solution from scratch for each round is very slow and so it is important to develop algorithms which can quickly update the solution with the new design matrix. Our main result is a dynamic tree data structure where any update to a single matrix can be propagated quickly throughout the tree. We show that our data structure can be used to solve dynamic versions of not only Tensor Product Regression, but also Tensor Product Spline regression (which is a generalization of ridge regression) and for maintaining Low Rank Approximations for the tensor product.

items.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
items.description: arXiv:2310.10239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

items.title: Point2SSM++: Self-Supervised Learning of Anatomical Shape Models from Point Clouds
items.description: arXiv:2405.09707v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) stands as a powerful technology for morphometric analysis in clinical research. SSM facilitates population-level characterization and quantification of anatomical shapes such as bones and organs, aiding in pathology and disease diagnostics and treatment planning. Despite its potential, SSM remains under-utilized in medical research due to the significant overhead associated with automatic construction methods, which demand complete, aligned shape surface representations. Additionally, optimization-based techniques rely on bias-inducing assumptions or templates and have prolonged inference times as the entire cohort is simultaneously optimized. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Point2SSM++, a principled, self-supervised deep learning approach that directly learns correspondence points from point cloud representations of anatomical shapes. Point2SSM++ is robust to misaligned and inconsistent input, providing SSM that accurately samples individual shape surfaces while effectively capturing population-level statistics. Furthermore, we present extensions of Point2SSM++ tailored for dynamic spatiotemporal and multi-anatomy scenarios, showcasing the broad versatility of the framework. Through extensive validation across diverse anatomies, evaluation metrics, and clinically relevant downstream tasks, we demonstrate Point2SSM++'s superiority over existing state-of-the-art deep learning models and the traditional approach. Point2SSM++ substantially enhances the feasibility of SSM generation and significantly broadens its array of potential clinical applications.

items.title: ADformer: A Multi-Granularity Spatial-Temporal Transformer for EEG-Based Alzheimer Detection
items.description: arXiv:2409.00032v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electroencephalography has emerged as a cost-effective, efficient tool to help neurologists detect Alzheimer's Disease. However, most existing approaches rely heavily on manual feature engineering or data transformation. While these techniques may help with small-scale datasets, they often cause information loss and distortion when applied to large-scale data, ultimately limiting model performance. Moreover, the limited subject scale and demographic diversity of datasets used in prior studies hinder comprehensive evaluation of model robustness and generalizability, thus restricting their applicability in real-world clinical settings. To address these challenges, we propose ADformer, a novel multi-granularity spatial-temporal transformer that captures both temporal and spatial features from raw EEG signals, enabling effective end-to-end representation learning. Our model introduces multi-granularity embedding strategies across both spatial and temporal dimensions, leveraging a two-stage intra-inter-granularity self-attention mechanism to learn local patterns within each granularity and global dependencies across granularities. We evaluate ADformer on 4 large-scale datasets totaling 1,713 subjects, one of the largest corpora for EEG-based AD detection to date, under a cross-validated, subject-independent setting. Experimental results demonstrate that ADformer consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving subject-level F1 scores of 87.11%, 89.83%, 67.99%, and 84.42% on the 4 datasets, respectively, in distinguishing Alzheimer's Disease patients from healthy control subjects.

items.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
items.description: arXiv:2412.08534v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance. We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution. To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

items.title: A Unifying Framework for Robust and Efficient Inference with Unstructured Data
items.description: arXiv:2505.00282v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI can cheaply extract structured variables from unstructured data, with alternative implementation choices potentially yielding different measures of the same concept. This creates a credibility challenge, effectively moving specification search upstream. We confront this challenge with MAR-S (Missing At Random Structured Data), a framework which adapts semiparametric missing data theory to deliver valid, efficient, robust inference with AI predictions. MAR-S anchors measurement in a transparent validation sample design, while AI scales measurement. We provide general recipes for MAR-S estimation and extend the framework to aggregated and transformed AI predictions, a common setting not addressed by existing frameworks.

items.title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
items.description: arXiv:2505.06927v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.

items.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
items.description: arXiv:2507.20560v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Privacy preservation in machine learning, particularly through Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), is crucial for analyzing sensitive data. However, existing statistical inference methods for SGD predominantly focus on cyclic subsampling, while DP-SGD requires randomized subsampling. This paper first bridges this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of SGD under the randomized rule and extending these results to DP-SGD. For DP-SGD, we show that the asymptotic variance decomposes into statistical, sampling, and privacy-induced components. We propose two methods for constructing valid confidence intervals: the plug-in method and the random scaling method. We also perform extensive numerical analysis showing that the proposed confidence intervals achieve nominal coverage rates while maintaining privacy.

items.title: StochEP: Stochastic Equilibrium Propagation for Spiking Convergent Recurrent Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2511.11320v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, sparse, biologically inspired computation. Training them with Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) and surrogate gradients achieves strong performance but remains biologically implausible. Equilibrium Propagation (EP) provides a more local and biologically grounded alternative. However, existing EP frameworks for SNNs largely rely on deterministic neurons, which require complex mechanisms to handle spiking discontinuities and do not scale beyond simple benchmarks such as MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Inspired by the stochastic nature of biological spiking mechanism and recent hardware trends, we propose a stochastic EP framework that integrates probabilistic spiking neurons into the EP paradigm. This formulation smoothens the optimization landscape, stabilizes training, and enables efficient and scalable learning in SNNs. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed stochastic EP dynamics approximate deterministic EP under mean-field theory, thereby inheriting its underlying theoretical guarantees. The proposed framework narrows the performance gap with both BPTT-trained SNNs and EP-trained non-spiking convergent recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) on CIFAR-10, DVS Gesture, and IMDB datasets, while preserving temporal and spatial locality. Our results highlight stochastic EP as a promising approach for neuromorphic and on-chip learning.

items.title: db-SP: Accelerating Sparse Attention for Visual Generative Models with Dual-Balanced Sequence Parallelism
items.description: arXiv:2511.23113v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scaling Diffusion Transformer (DiT) inference via sequence parallelism is critical for reducing latency in visual generation, but is severely hampered by workload imbalance when applied to models employing block-wise sparse attention. The imbalance stems from the inherent variation in sparsity across attention heads and the irregular distribution of dense blocks within the sparse mask, when sequence parallelism is applied along the head dimension (as in Ulysses) or the block dimension (as in Ring Attention). In this paper, we formalize a sparse imbalance ratio to quantify the imbalance, and propose db-SP, a sparsity-aware sequence parallelism technique that tackles the challenge. db-SP contains a dual-level partitioning approach that achieves near-perfect workload balance at both the head and block levels with negligible overhead. Furthermore, to handle the evolving sparsity patterns across denoising steps and layers, db-SP dynamically determines the parallel degrees for the head and block dimensions at runtime. Experimental results demonstrate that db-SP delivers an end-to-end speedup of 1.25x and an attention-specific speedup of 1.40x over state-of-the-art sequence parallel methods on average. Code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/db-SP.

items.title: BayesFlow 2: Multi-Backend Amortized Bayesian Inference in Python
items.description: arXiv:2602.07098v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern Bayesian inference involves a mixture of computational methods for estimating, validating, and drawing conclusions from probabilistic models as part of principled workflows. An overarching motif of many Bayesian methods is that they are relatively slow, which often becomes prohibitive when fitting complex models to large data sets. Amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) offers a path to solving the computational challenges of Bayes. ABI trains neural networks on model simulations, rewarding users with rapid inference of any model-implied quantity, such as point estimates, likelihoods, or full posterior distributions. In this work, we present the Python library BayesFlow, Version 2, for general-purpose ABI. Along with direct posterior, likelihood, and ratio estimation, the software includes support for multiple popular deep learning backends, a rich collection of generative networks for sampling and density estimation, complete customization and high-level interfaces, as well as new capabilities for hyperparameter optimization, design optimization, and multilevel modeling. Using a case study on dynamical system parameter estimation, combined with comparisons to similar software, we show that our streamlined, user-friendly workflow has strong potential to support broad adoption.

items.title: Learned Finite Element-based Regularization of the Inverse Problem in Electrocardiographic Imaging
items.description: arXiv:2602.07466v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) seeks to reconstruct cardiac electrical activity from body-surface potentials noninvasively. However, the associated inverse problem is severely ill-posed and requires robust regularization. While classical approaches primarily employ spatial smoothing, the temporal structure of cardiac dynamics remains underexploited despite its physiological relevance. We introduce a space-time regularization framework that couples spatial regularization with a learned temporal Fields-of-Experts (FoE) prior to capture complex spatiotemporal activation patterns. We derive a finite element discretization on unstructured cardiac surface meshes, prove Mosco-convergence, and develop a scalable optimization algorithm capable of handling the FoE term. Numerical experiments on synthetic epicardial data demonstrate improved denoising and inverse reconstructions compared to handcrafted spatiotemporal methods, yielding solutions that are both robust to noise and physiologically plausible.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
items.description: arXiv:2604.02507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This survey provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from AI feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.

items.title: When the Prior Is Wrong: Probing Misspecified Diffusion Priors in Inverse Problems
items.description: arXiv:2604.21066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While diffusion priors generate high-quality posterior samples across many scientific inverse problems, they are often trained on purely simulated data, thus inheriting the errors and biases of these underlying sources. Many approaches to adapting diffusion priors from a single observation require sufficient conflict between the data and the prior to successfully adapt and do not allow specific misspecification hypotheses to be tested. On the other hand, existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods determine whether the observation is compatible with a fixed prior, rather than specifying which assumptions to relax or by how much. To address these issues, we propose PIVOT: Prior Inference Via Observation-driven Transformations, which formulates diffusion prior misspecification as inference over an underlying latent variable representing a scientifically plausible discrepancy. By expanding the prior along these plausible directions of misspecification, PIVOT infers a posterior over the strength of each proposed discrepancy given the observation. This process can be efficiently amortized with just one posterior sampling pass using a conditional diffusion model. We also demonstrate how to determine if a proposed discrepancy is inconclusive because the measurement is too noisy or ill-posed. We validate PIVOT on seismic imaging and real-world black hole imaging problems, where we find that OOD observations generally lead to larger perturbation strengths when the proposed discrepancy family captures relevant components of the mismatch, as long as the discrepancy is visible to the measurement. PIVOT thereby provides an interpretable probe into how real-world priors could be misspecified.

items.title: Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching
items.description: arXiv:2605.12951v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching (CCVFM), a generative model that augments hierarchical rectified flow with a data-informed source distribution. Standard flow matching regresses only the conditional mean of the velocity; hierarchical flow matching instead models the full conditional velocity law with a second, inner flow in velocity space, but this inner flow is asked to transport isotropic Gaussian noise to a multimodal target velocity distribution from scratch. Our key observation is that this inner source can be replaced by a closed-form surrogate built from a coreset of the target. CCVFM first compresses the target into weighted atoms using an entropic Sinkhorn coreset and lifts them to a Gaussian mixture. The induced conditional velocity law is then a closed-form Gaussian mixture that can be sampled without a learned neural sampler. A lightweight correction flow, trained from this surrogate source, then refines the remaining surrogate-to-target residual rather than learning an entire noise-to-data map. We prove that the surrogate transport cost equals the target-surrogate Wasserstein gap under an explicit compression assumption, whereas the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale lower bound. We further characterize the conditional second moment of the training target when the source velocity is drawn from the surrogate law independently of the target velocity, and show that the part of it that depends on the source is small when the surrogate conditional law is close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance. Empirically, on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and CelebA-HQ, the proposed method reaches competitive few-step generation under matched architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM.

items.title: Hyrax: An Extensible Framework for Rapid ML Experimentation and Unsupervised Discovery in the Era of Rubin, Roman, and Euclid
items.description: arXiv:2605.18959v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Roman Space Telescope, Euclid, and other next-generation surveys will deliver imaging, spectroscopic, and time-domain data at scales that increasingly shift the bottleneck in astronomical machine learning (ML) projects from model design to infrastructure. We present Hyrax, an open-source, modular, GPU-enabled Python framework that supports the full ML lifecycle in astronomy: from data acquisition and training to inference and experiment comparison, with capabilities including multimodal dataset support, integrated vector databases for similarity search, and interactive two- and three-dimensional latent-space exploration for unsupervised discovery. We demonstrate Hyrax's versatility through five representative applications on real survey data: (i) unsupervised representation learning on $\sim 4\times10^5$ Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Data Preview 1 (DP1) galaxies, surfacing new merger and low-surface-brightness candidates missing from reference Euclid and Dark Energy Survey catalogs, while also isolating imaging artifacts -- all without labeled training data; (ii) hybrid density-based clustering for identifying cluster-scale gravitational lens candidates in DP1 data; (iii) multimodal early-time transient classification in the Zwicky Transient Facility leveraging light curves, spectra, images, and metadata; (iv) supervised false-positive filtering in shift-and-stack searches for distant solar system objects in the Dark Energy Camera Ecliptic Exploration Project survey; and (v) supervised detection of semi-resolved dwarf galaxies in Hyper Suprime-Cam and LSST-like imaging using synthetic source injection. Together, these results demonstrate that Hyrax provides astronomy-specific ML infrastructure that enables systematic discovery and rapid methodological iteration across next-generation astronomical surveys.

items.title: Resolution-free neural surrogates for geometric parameterization and mapping with spatially varying fields
items.description: arXiv:2605.28551v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many imaging problems require computing spatial transformations induced by spatially varying intensity, feature, or density fields. Canonical examples include distortion correction, deformable image registration, atlas-based segmentation, and deformation-driven image analysis. These tasks can be formulated as geometric mapping problems in which the transformation is constrained to preserve local structure, control boundary behavior, or regulate angular distortion. Such formulations typically lead to variational models, diffusion processes, or elliptic partial differential equations. However, repeatedly solving high-resolution systems becomes computationally expensive when the underlying parameter fields vary across instances. In this work, we propose a resolution-free neural surrogate for geometric parameterization and mapping problems. Given a spatially varying parameter field $p:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^m$ and grid nodes $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^N\subset\Omega$, the model predicts mapped locations $\{u(x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ on structured grids of different sizes without retraining. To avoid dependence on a fixed grid, we use a multi-resolution geometric encoding strategy that conditions the network on coordinate-augmented samples of the parameter field. The model is trained without labeled solution data by enforcing geometry-aware constraints derived from variational energies, diffusion-based density equalization, and quasi-conformal theory. Experimental results on quasi-conformal mapping and density-equalizing mapping problems are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

items.title: AlloGen: Conformation-Selective Binder Generation with Differential State Scoring
items.description: arXiv:2606.05474v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Protein binder design commonly optimizes compatibility with a single receptor conformation, leaving preference over alternative functional states unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce AlloGen, a modular method that decouples backbone generation from state-selectivity scoring. We train its SE(3)-invariant interface graph transformer, $Q_\theta$, through interface-quality regression followed by paired conformational discrimination. By comparing scores across states, we rerank candidates and guide frozen backbone generators without retraining. On a benchmark of 65 targets spanning 15 protein families, $Q_\theta$ achieved a mean Spearman correlation of $0.520$ on eight held-out targets. All 15 evaluated generator-guidance combinations achieved positive predicted selectivity averaged over these targets, and RFdiffusion with Langevin refinement reached $\bar{S}_{\mathrm{cons}}=0.677$ on calmodulin (CaM). To test the predicted preference experimentally, we measured binding by bio-layer interferometry. Five designed peptides bound holo CaM, with the strongest measured $K_D$ of 46.6 nM, and none showed detectable apo CaM binding under the tested conditions. Together, these results support computational prioritization of conformation-selective binders.

items.title: Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting with a Multi-GPU PyTorch Backend
items.description: arXiv:2606.11390v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gaussian splatting methods have become increasingly popular for neural reconstruction of the real world. However, they are often limited in scale and resolution due to compute and memory constraints. We present a multi-GPU Gaussian splatting approach that scales reconstruction to higher resolutions and larger scenes while abstracting away the code complexity typically associated with distributing a model. We demonstrate city-scale reconstructions with street-level detail consisting of over 1 billion Gaussian splats. To accomplish this, we propose a PyTorch backend that distributes parameters and operators across GPUs via CUDA unified memory, with optional NVLink support. Because distribution occurs at the operator level, the model code requires no explicit cross-device communication. More broadly, the backend exposes multiple GPUs as an aggregate asynchronous PyTorch device and supports a broad set of PyTorch operators enabling the distribution of general PyTorch workloads.

items.title: Unsupervised Detection of Underground Tunnels in Ground-Penetrating Radar Using Depth-Restricted Reconstruction Scoring
items.description: arXiv:2607.04882v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hand-dug tunnels that reach buried pipelines from below are hard to find before they are used, and too rare to train a supervised detector. The engineering application of this work is detecting such tunnels in ground-penetrating radar surveys of a monitored site. The contribution in artificial intelligence is a detection scheme that needs no tunnel examples: a convolutional autoencoder learns the site's normal ground from surveys recorded before any tunnel exists, later survey windows are scored by their largest reconstruction errors within the travel-time band where a tunnel can lie, and evaluation holds out whole survey lines. On field data from a tunnel hand-dug for this study (0.6 m wide, 1 m high, roof 0.9-1.4 m deep) and surveyed repeatedly with a 250-megahertz radar in dry and wet conditions, the detector reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994 and an F1 score of 0.972 on 1,600 test windows and flags all 29 tunnel crossings. Restricting the score to the depth band improves all six detectors tested and, with a quarter of the training data, outperforms whole-window scoring trained on all of it; the best rule for the same band without learning misses 9 of the 29 crossings. On two unseen plots, false alarms stay at 1.6% on comparable ground but reach 9.3% on irrigated soil; recalibrating the threshold on a fifth of that plot's lines lowers them to 4.2%, retraining brings no significant further reduction, and models trained there alone still detect the original tunnel.

items.title: Near-Optimal Learning of Gaussian Sobolev Operators
items.description: arXiv:2607.11921v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A key question in operator learning is how to design surrogate operators with provable approximation guarantees in reasonable computational time. Whereas holomorphic operators can be approximated efficiently, i.e., with at least algebraic convergence in the number of training samples, learning finitely regular operators is known to be less efficient. The reason is an intrinsic curse of sample complexity, which allows only subalgebraic convergence rates. This fact makes it all the more important to develop algorithms which provably achieve these rates. In this work, we present a fully data-driven algorithm, termed Hermite-PCA approximation, for learning Gaussian Sobolev operators with near-optimal sample complexity. It employs principal component analysis and weighted least-squares methods and is therefore computationally efficient. Moreover, it is spectral, in the sense that it achieves faster (and near-optimal) convergence as the Sobolev regularity increases. We provide a full error analysis of this algorithm along with numerical experiments that match our theoretical results and empirically confirm the efficacy of Hermite-PCA approximation for learning Sobolev operators.

items.title: Toward Energy-Efficient and Low-Power Arrhythmia Detection for Wearable Devices
items.description: arXiv:2607.14747v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, and conditions such as arrhythmia often require long-term monitoring for effective detection and diagnosis. However, current wearable monitoring devices are bulky, uncomfortable, and typically rely on clinicians to manually evaluate electrocardiograms (ECGs). While Deep Learning (DL) algorithms have shown superior performance in arrhythmia detection and classification, their computational complexity coupled with high power consumption limit deployment in wearable devices. To address this challenge, this paper investigates the use of approximation techniques to reduce the power and energy consumption of DL architectures while maintaining acceptable classification performance. Specifically, techniques such as data precision reduction and approximate multiplication are investigated in a state-of-the-art DL model and its corresponding hardware architecture. The model is trained and validated using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, and hardware implementations employing various approximate multipliers are synthesized and evaluated. Compared with the state-of-the-art 8.75 {\mu}W (and 2.08 {\mu}J) reference architecture, our proposed architecture consumes 3.07 {\mu}W (and 2.17 {\mu}J) at 12 kHz, showing 64.9% reduction in power consumption while providing an acceptable output quality, i.e., 93.7% classification accuracy and 92.1% sensitivity. At 100 MHz, our proposed architecture consumes 9.45 mW (and 0.8 {\mu}J), showing 61.5% reduction in energy consumption as compared to the state-of-the-art architecture. These results demonstrate that our proposed approximations significantly extend wearable device battery life while preserving the required arrhythmia classification performance.

items.title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification
items.description: arXiv:2607.15832v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate in the noiseless setting. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.

items.title: QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing
items.description: arXiv:2607.21411v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum transfer learning (QTL) is commonly evaluated by replacing a classical classifier with a fixed variational quantum head, leaving unclear when quantum inference provides measurable benefit. We propose QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing, which retains high-confidence classical predictions and routes low-confidence samples to a quantum fallback. Using a frozen ResNet18 backbone, we compare manually designed QTL heads, architecture-searched KetGPT heads, and parameter-matched classical baselines under consistent experimental settings. On Fashion-MNIST, standard QTL heads reach at most 59.7% accuracy and 0.564 F1-score, whereas compact KetGPT Candidate #160 reaches 80.2% accuracy and 0.800 F1-score. On the routed low-confidence subset, Candidate #160 improves accuracy over the matched MLP by 6.31, 5.38, and 3.73 percentage points at \tau=0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, respectively. At the selected operating point \tau=0.70, the adaptive system reaches 81.78% accuracy and 0.816 F1-score while routing only 36.12% of test samples to the quantum branch. Candidate #160 uses 10 quantum parameters and 9 gates, while experiments on CIFAR-10, KMNIST, and SVHN show consistent accuracy gains over the corresponding adaptive classical baselines. These results show that selective quantum invocation can reduce quantum execution while improving inference on low-confidence samples.

items.title: Reducing Fixed-Batch Client Idleness in Many-Client Edge Split Learning
items.description: arXiv:2609.29395v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parallel Split Learning with Global Sampling (GPSL) trains a split model on a fixed-size batch drawn from the data of all clients. When the client population is much larger than the batch, most clients contribute no data in a round, and additional server capacity does not change this. We propose Global Clustered Parallel Split Learning (GCPSL), which assigns clients to stable clusters, runs one GPSL workload per cluster concurrently, and periodically fuses the split-model replicas. We derive the expected direct data participation under the batch sampler, which separates repeated sampling of the same clients from idling at the fusion barrier. With 256 clients, more clusters raise participation but reduce the client diversity seen by each workload. In three paired runs on four H100 GPUs, GCPSL raises direct data participation from 22% to 57-60%. With random or size-balanced clusters, it reaches 85% CIFAR-10 validation accuracy in 5.7 minutes, 1.6 times faster than GPSL with its batch sharded across the same GPUs. It matches per-step synchronized data-parallel GPSL at 85% and reaches 88% in about 10 instead of 19.5 minutes, without per-step global gradient or BatchNorm synchronization. Concurrent execution is 3.11 times faster than sequential execution of the same workloads.

items.title: Conformal Prediction and Conditional Coverage for Tabular Foundation Models
items.description: arXiv:2609.34887v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) provide predictive distributions for regression, but their prediction regions can exhibit undercoverage or overcoverage even when point predictions are accurate. We introduce C-USIM (Conditionally-Uniformized Score Integration Method), a lightweight application of highest predictive density split conformal prediction that accommodates multimodal predictions. Given calibration and test outputs, it requires no additional training or model inference. It provides finite-sample marginal validity under our assumptions. We bound conditional-marginal coverage gaps using distribution-estimation error and score discreteness, and examine coverage heterogeneity through percentile rank-score plots. Experiments with TabPFN and TabICL show improved marginal coverage accuracy and lower average conditional and group coverage errors. Under a fixed data budget, allocating more observations to calibration can reduce marginal coverage error despite less accurate point predictions.

items.title: RNA Design via Conditioned Flow Matching and Finite-Policy Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2609.36885v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: RNA design aims to identify sequences that fold into specified secondary structures. Existing methods formulate the task as target-specific search or conditional generation. However, natural RNA evolution proceeds through sequence variation and selection, with compensatory substitutions, whereas these methods do not explicitly model this process. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage framework comprising RNA Inverse-Folding Flow (RNA-IFlow) and RNA-IFlow-RL. RNA-IFlow uses structure-conditioned Dirichlet Flow Matching to model coordinated variation across the sequence, while RNA-IFlow-RL maps the learned flow to a pairing-preserving finite policy and refines it with thermodynamic feedback. Our framework achieves leading performance on multiple benchmarks, reaching 85.19% Pass@1 on Rfam-27. Further analyses reveal thermodynamic gains, policy dynamics, and robustness across settings. Our work couples coordinated variation with thermodynamic selection, offering a novel paradigm for RNA design.

items.title: VirusCascade: Hijacking Collaborative Reflection in LLM-Powered Recommender Agents
items.description: arXiv:2609.38270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advancing beyond traditional static scoring models, LLM-powered agentic recommender systems (LLM-ARS) instantiate users and items as autonomous agents, whose semantic states are dynamically refined through a recurrent process known as collaborative reflection. While this mechanism improves recommendation quality, it simultaneously introduces a systemic vulnerability: adversarial evidence injected into a single agent can be rationalised into a legitimate preference narrative, written back into memory, and propagated to other agents through interaction contexts. We term the local rationalisation process reflection laundering, and its system-wide escalation through collaborative reflection collaborative-reflection hijacking. Existing attacks on recommender systems, whether based on interaction-level data poisoning or text-level adversarial perturbations, assume static pipelines and thus cannot exploit this recurrent, multi-agent amplification pathway. To bridge this gap, we first conduct a controlled vulnerability analysis that establishes two exploitable properties underlying collaborative-reflection hijacking: reflective persistence and cross-agent propagation. Then building on these findings, we propose VirusCascade, the first black-box targeted promotion attack that jointly shapes semantic and structural attack surfaces: the former ensures the target item is naturally rationalised as satisfying broad user preferences, the latter positions it for system-wide propagation. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets across diverse LLM-ARS architectures demonstrate that VirusCascade consistently achieves state-of-the-art targeted exposure under evaluated stealth constraints, reaching a mean E@20 of 0.384 and surpassing the strongest baseline by an absolute margin of +0.185.

items.title: GazeFlow: From Human Gaze Behavior to Generative Egocentric Gaze Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2609.38519v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Egocentric gaze prediction enables many downstream applications but remains challenging, as human gaze is inherently stochastic. This stochasticity is constrained by structured temporal dynamics alternating between fixations and saccades, top-down influences from tasks, and bottom-up visual saliency. Based on this observation, we introduce GazeFlow, a framework that directly models gaze as a joint distribution of temporal gaze positions conditioned upon both top-down and bottom-up information. In particular, GazeFlow uses conditional flow matching (CFM): a learned velocity field iteratively transports a Gaussian noise sample into a plausible gaze trajectory drawn from this joint distribution. The velocity field is conditioned on bottom-up visual features extracted by a video encoder and on top-down task information obtained by globally querying these features. On standard datasets, GazeFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance on per-frame metrics, and the generated trajectories align better with human gaze temporal dynamics. The project page and source code are at: https://horizon-lab.org/gazeflow/

items.title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
items.description: arXiv:2610.00636v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. We extend the benchmark to four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. In a workflow, the agent runs all simulations itself. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on nine LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 62.8-97.9% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the stronger agents fall only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes more failures to scientific errors than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

items.title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.09335v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

items.title: Extreme Binary Classification: Extreme Value Theory for Extreme Constraint on False Negative
items.description: arXiv:2610.09984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While binary classification is one of the most extensively studied problems in machine learning, the regime in which the goal is to learn a classifier with an almost zero false negative rate remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce the Extreme Binary Classification problem, where the objective is to learn a classifier whose false negative rate $\alpha$ is constrained by $\epsilon_{N_1}=o_{N_1\to\infty}(1/N_1)$, with $N_1$ denoting the number of positive examples in the training set. To address this problem, we propose a threshold adaptation method theoretically grounded in guarantees derived from Extreme Value Theory, together with a feature selection procedure based on a permutation test applied to sample maxima. Experimental results on four real-world datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that our approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods. In addition, we illustrate its interpretability through an application to a cancer screening dataset.

items.title: Minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap of continuous Markov chains, with applications to empirical concentration bounds
items.description: arXiv:2610.20007v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap $\gamma_{ps}$ of a Markov chain from the observation of a single trajectory. Extending earlier works on finite-state space chains by Wolfer and Kontorovich (2024), we provide an estimator in the case of a compact, continuous state-space. Our estimator appears to be minimax-optimal on the class of chains with a transition operator with Lipschitz density, up to logarithmic terms. Our estimator, combined with Paulin's version of Bernstein inequality, allows to derive empirical concentration inequalities for Markov chains. This unlocks many applications, from confidence intervals, to active learning and generalization bounds. In particular, for rested bandits with Markov rewards, we provide a version of UCB with a regret bound similar to the one in the iid case, without assuming any knowledge on the pseudo-spectral gap of the chains.

items.title: L2GSSL: Label-Efficient Local-to-Global Self-Supervised Learning for Volumetric Healthcare Data
items.description: arXiv:2610.21356v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Healthcare institutions routinely accumulate high-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, but only a fraction can be annotated by experts. We present L2GSSL, a local-to-global self-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled volumes by decomposing pretraining into intra-slice and inter-slice representation spaces. A slice encoder learns view-invariant local features, and a global encoder aggregates the resulting tokens to model volumetric context. The stop-gradient isolates the local space from the global objective, while slice-wise execution and a three-phase schedule support training under constrained GPU memory. On LIDC-IDRI lung nodule malignancy classification, L2GSSL reaches $0.9229$ AUROC with only $10\%$ of the labels and $0.9377$ with $25\%$, exceeding the volume-level VICReg by $0.0229$ and $0.0294$, respectively. With all labels, the strongest supervised baseline exceeds L2GSSL by only $0.0044$ AUROC, consistent with self-supervised pretraining providing its greatest value when annotations are limited. A model fine-tuned on $25\%$ of LIDC-IDRI and evaluated on the external LNDb cohort without further training obtains $0.8138$ AUROC and $0.7589$ AUPRC, improving over the strongest evaluated self-supervised baseline by $0.1130$ and $0.0954$. Experiments across data sources, thoracic and abdominal anatomy, downstream tasks, and two backbones examine healthcare-data variety, while masking malignant lesion-bearing slices at inference sharply reduces performance, indicating that predictions rely substantially on lesion content.

items.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
items.description: arXiv:2610.25997v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.96 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

items.title: High-Order Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions on Manifolds
items.description: arXiv:2610.27022v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study high-order Gaussian approximation for Besov functions $f\in B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$ with $\alpha>0$ on a compact smooth embedded manifold $X$ without boundary. For $r<\alpha$, a suitable signed combination of Gaussian integral operators at different bandwidths gives an $H^r(X)$ error bounded by $C\gamma^{\alpha-r}\|f\|_{B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)}$. The squared Gaussian RKHS norm of the approximant is bounded by $C\gamma^{-\varrho}\|f\|_{L_2(X)}^2$, where $\varrho$ is the intrinsic dimension of $X$. We apply these approximation results to two statistical learning problems. For regularized Gaussian logistic classification, we combine the approximation bounds with a localized oracle inequality. For a potentially unbounded Bayes function in $B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$ and a marginal density in $L_p(X)$, the excess logistic risk has upper bounds of order $((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n)^{2\beta/(2\beta+3\varrho)}$ for the unclipped predictor and $((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n)^{\beta/(\beta+\varrho)}$ for clipped predictions with suitably selected parameters, where $\beta=2\alpha(1-1/p)$. Under bounded marginal densities, our excess misclassification risk bound matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical H\"older-class exponent. For elliptic operator learning, we assemble a Gaussian Galerkin solution operator from random manifold samples. Its error in the operator norm from $B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$ to $H^1(X)$ is bounded with high probability by two terms. The trial-space term has a decay exponent in the number of Gaussian centers that can approach $(\alpha+1)/\varrho$. The bias and sampling term is of order $n^{-2N/(4N+\varrho)}$ for a fixed trial space, where $n$ is the number of sample pairs and $N$ is the number of Gaussian scales used for matrix assembly. The convergence rates for both problems depend on the intrinsic dimension $\varrho$ and are independent of the ambient dimension $d$.

items.title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.06732v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

items.title: Ostinato: Low-Latency CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents
items.description: arXiv:2611.11533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on local workstations with consumer GPUs, where quantized mixture-of-experts (MoE) models split routed experts between GPU and host memory. Prefix-cached agent sessions alternate single-token decode with short tool-return prefills, typically up to a few hundred tokens. Short tool turns touch more experts than consumer GPUs can hold, yet direct roughly 85% of DeepSeek-V4-Flash's routes to a static GPU pool while leaving 3.3-5.5 tokens per cold expert. Widely used local engines such as llama.cpp and KTransformers either copy tens of gigabytes over PCIe per turn, compute every route on the CPU while idling resident GPU experts, or budget GPU memory by whole layers and uniform per-layer quotas. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE engine that reuses one static cross-layer GPU pool in place across every forward pass. During decode and short tool turns, Ostinato computes resident routes on the GPUs and sparse cold routes on the CPU, so short turns copy no expert weights; on long prefills, it deduplicates cold uploads; and for multi-GPU decode, all-zero expert slots with device-side synchronization capture each GPU's decode step in one CUDA graph. Across held-out SWE and -bench sessions on three MoE models, Ostinato cuts median tool-turn waits by 2.5-6.6x and finishes sessions 1.36-3.83x faster than default baselines, staying 1.30-1.94x faster when baselines align their upload threshold and weight loading. It finishes sessions fastest across seven agent workloads, one to four GPUs, and up to eight concurrent sessions, while its cross-layer pool speeds up 335 GB DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.81-2.19x over llama.cpp's expert cache.

items.title: Whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1 depends on a normalisation convention: evidence from two fMRI datasets
items.description: arXiv:2611.15533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival or beat trained networks as models of primary visual cortex (V1), and we had reported such an advantage in THINGS fMRI. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the trained network was ahead at every pooling grid in THINGS and in NSD (8 of 8 subjects), also when voxel responses were centred within runs. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) in THINGS depended on analysis choices (28 analyses: intervals above 0 in 5, below 0 in 9, including 0 in 14); in NSD with its standard normalisation, none of 28 analyses favoured the untrained network. The untrained advantage appears when a response profile common to all trials is left in the voxel patterns and model units are not centred, under correlation distance: removing the session-mean profile in THINGS reduced it from +0.030 to +0.005; with raw betas it reached +0.100 in THINGS, appeared in the THINGS test images, and appeared in NSD (+0.116, 8 of 8 subjects, a pre-specified prediction), where it was confined to this one of 28 analyses. With the profile left in, both representational dissimilarity matrices are dominated by per-image response amplitude, which in V1 tracks contrast energy, and the untrained network's matrix is more amplitude-dominated; the amplitude itself is matched equally by both networks; removing the amplitude structure from both matrices removes the advantage in NSD (+0.116 to -0.009, 8 of 8 subjects). A luminance-and-contrast baseline outperformed every network under ridge in both datasets (point estimates); the networks reached 10-15% of the NSD noise-ceiling lower bound. 24 of 88 pre-specified predictions were not met. We recommend centring or normalising voxel responses within session, reporting the sensitivity of RSA rankings to this choice and to model-unit centring, and replicating on a second dataset.

items.title: Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting
items.description: arXiv:2611.28321v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.

items.title: Inferring Experimental Objectives in Microscopy Experiments from Decision Traces
items.description: arXiv:2611.29814v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern microscopes can acquire, analyze and act on data far faster than human operators can decide what to measure next. Exploiting this speed in automated experiments requires the instrument to follow the scientific logic of the operator, and one way to encode that logic is through reward functions that become part of the operation process. Here we explore whether such reward functions can be learned from the decision histories of microscope operators. We propose multiple frameworks in which recorded choices among alternative measurement locations serve as comparative evidence about the operator's preferences, and we compare several algorithms for reconstructing the reward including interpretable linear models built on physically meaningful image descriptors, nonlinear functions of the same descriptors, an unsupervised image representation followed by preference modeling, and a preference trained deep kernel inspired model. The result of this analysis is a spatial field of reward functions over the sample that can be used to run the instrument. We also propose a way to benchmark these approaches, based on withheld decisions and on decision histories generated with known objectives. We then examine the possibility that a decision history contains changing priorities throughout the experiment. A hidden Markov model assigns distinct rewards to recurring selection strategies, whereas a continuous-state model tracks smoothly varying preference weights. Controlled sequences generated over real microscopy candidate sets show that both concealed switches and gradual drift can be recovered. These reward functions, learned directly from recorded decisions, provide candidate objectives for future automated microscopy experiments.

items.title: Sampling with graph wavelet kernels: optimality and adaptivity to regularity and geometry
items.description: arXiv:2611.29992v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-H\"older and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-H\"older observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

items.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
items.description: arXiv:2611.32595v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that the following problem is NEXPTIME-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and truncated ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.

items.title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
items.description: Drone attacks on data centers. Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion. In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine: We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there's an incentive to target it. Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers: Read full article Comments

items.title: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
items.description: A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary. I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable. This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system. Build evidence before choosing a target The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting. Before you recommend a change, build a small evidence inventory: Manifests, lockfiles, entry points, and deployable components Verified commands for installing, building, testing, packaging, and running Runtime pins in containers, CI workflows, deployment files, and developer tooling External contracts such as APIs, database behavior, file formats, and user workflows End-of-life frameworks and dependencies, with evidence that the application still uses them Record uncertainty while you work. I use three simple labels: documented, inferred, and unverified. If two files disagree about the Java version, resolve the contradiction. If you can’t determine whether a CI check blocks merges, say so. Record the unknown rather than treating a guess as a finding. That inventory gives you something concrete to review with the people who own the application before you propose changes. Choose the least disruptive treatment that works Once you understand the application, make the decision per component. A single system can contain code that should stay, dependencies that should be swapped, and one subsystem that genuinely needs a rewrite. First, check whether a capability is still needed. Remove it only after verifying that it is unused or superseded and confirming that decision with its owner. Removal is a separate decision, and it’s not necessarily the most disruptive one. For a capability you still need, start with the option that changes the least: Keep it. Supported code that still fits the job doesn’t need a modernization story. Upgrade it. Move to a supported major version and fix the breaking changes. Swap it. Replace an abandoned dependency while preserving the existing design. Wrap it. Stabilize a useful interface and replace the internals in increments. Rewrite it. Use this when no responsible upgrade path exists or the architecture cannot meet the requirement. This is a decision order, not a universal ranking of effort or risk. Ask what evidence justifies choosing a more disruptive option. “The code is old” is not enough. A known vulnerability with no patched release for the pinned version, a dependency that fails on the required runtime, or a measured reliability target the current design cannot meet can justify escalation. Decide what proof is possible The next question is whether the component can run well enough to produce evidence, even if the legacy CI pipeline is not green. Run a time-boxed feasibility check. Try to install dependencies, build on an available toolchain, start the component, and execute at least one meaningful test. Stop when the time box expires. The result sends you down one of two paths. Capture behavior, then upgrade. Use this path when the old application can still run at an acceptable cost. Record its externally visible behavior, fix the test harness where practical, and use those checks to verify the upgrade. Build a small modern slice first. Use this path when the old component cannot run until you have already changed it. Move the thinnest useful workflow to supported technology, prove it, and expand from there. Requiring a complete legacy test suite in this situation is circular. Restoring the test suite is part of the modernization. I use the following safety levels, adapted from the doc-and-modernize skill , to describe the strongest regression protection available: Level Strongest honest protection L0 No usable regression net; treat the old code and available documentation as the specification. L1 Small reversible changes, old and new paths in parallel, smoke checks, and domain review. L2 Captured inputs and outputs, snapshots, or other behavioral comparisons. L3 Automated checks cover part of the system, with the remaining gaps named. L4 An automated CI gate combines lint, unit, behavioral, and end-to-end checks for the agreed scope. State what you can prove and what risk remains. Even an L4 gate cannot establish that every possible behavior is correct. APIs, database effects, files, rendered output, and business workflows often make durable comparison points because those behaviors can survive a framework or language change. PiggyMetrics: capture behavior, then upgrade PiggyMetrics was the clearest example of an application that looked worse than it was. The project used Java 8, Spring Boot 2.0.3, Spring Cloud Finchley, Zuul, Hystrix, and the old spring-security-oauth2 library. It would have been easy to call the application unworkable and start drawing a new architecture. The feasibility check told a different story.
